The Due d'Orleans' forthcoming • visit to the Queen at Balmoral has given rise to numerous ac- counts in the Parisian newspapers of at engage- ment between the young prince and one of her Majesty's granddaughters. Some of the playful scribes have selected among themselves the daughters a the Prince of Wales, Duke of Edin- burgh, and Princess Chrisian. The Due d'Orleans was once engaged to his cousin Princess Marguerite, but the match wai broken off by mutual consent.

France and the world have lost in the death of Renan one of the most brilliant writers of the age. It is as a writer rather than a philosopher that Renan made his mark. He enriched literature with many volumes which made him the first of French stylists, and he added to the thought of his time, but as a sceptical idealist he had no new doctrine to found. There is a Renanism, but the novelty is in the treat- ment of subjects rather than in the matter.

The Queen has entirely given up attending "pub- lic worship" on Sunday mornings in the parish kirk of Crathie, where 3he went regularly for thirty- 'ire years, except when the weather kept her at home. The rush of tourists from Braemar and Ballater be- came latterly an intolerable nuisance, and they olt-n behaved very badly. The Queen now goes to Cruthie only on the autumn "Sacrament Sabbath," which is usually the last Sunday in uctober. The church is a frightful building, and its only adorn- ment is a stained-glass window which the Queen erected to the memory of Dr. Norman Macleod. A private chapel has been added to Balmoral, which is known as tbe "worship room." The walls are panelled with Scotch fir from the Royal forest of Ballochbuie, which is beautifully polished, and the four mullioned windows are tilled with stained glass.

Mr. McGurrin, an American reporter, gave an ex- hibition at the Press Club, on Saturday night, on the typewriter, which certainly entitles him to be regarded as the Paderewski of the instrument. He wrote the line "Nos is the time for all good men to come to the aid of the party " at the rate of one hundred and forty-seven words a minute. This was not up to the anticipations formed of his lightning dexterity,but somewhat later in the even- ing Mr. McGurrin wrote the same sentence no less than thirteen times in one minute, or at a speed of two hundred and eight words. This is approaching the marvellous. From dictation Mr. McGurrin wrote one hundred and two words a minute, and ,ven blindfold—so sure was he of his keys—he totalled up one hundred and seventeen words in the same space of time. The operator "took " a Par- liamentary paper at the rate of sixty-eight words a minute and reported—and printed—a epeech at about a like rate. Even at the marvellous speed of two hundred and eight words in sixty seconds the ,vriting was clean, and almost without mistakes. --- Lord Donington i 3 the latest addition to the roll of English peers who hare gone over to Rome. There is something very strange about the conver- -ion. When Lord Donington's eldest son, the Earl .if Loudoun, married a Roman Catholic lady, Lord uonington was so incensed that he threatened to lcave every acre of the Clifton property, over which tie had control, away horn the title. The family quarrel was of long duration, and no one dreamed hat Lord Donington would be the one to give in. lie has, however, been won over to the faith to which he was formerly so hostile. Lord Donington is a man of great wealth, and is in the peculiar position of having an eldest son a rank higher in the peerage than himself.

It is rumoured in Dublin that Lord Houghton, the new Viceroy of Ireland, will very soon enter again the pleasant bonds of wedlock. Meanwhile his married sisters, the Hon. Mrs. Henniker and Lady Fitzgerald, will assist his Excellency in dis- charging the social functions of the Court in Dublin Castle and dispensing the hospitalities of the Vice- regal Lodge in the Plicenix Park. The Court is just as stiff, and stilted, and elaborate, with its formalities and its regulations as to precedence, if not quite so brilliant, as the Court at Windsor or at Buckingham Castle. The Viceregal household has its Chamberlain, its Gentleman Usher, Master of the Horse, Comptroller, Chaplain, Physician, Surgeon, Oculist. and enen a Dental Surgeon. The Lord Lieutenant is addressed as "Sir," just like the Prince of Wales—and he has the privilege of kissing the young ladies presented at the Drawing Rooms. Some of the past Lord Lieutenants have kissed as many as three hundred young ladies in the course of a single afternoon. His Excellency can accept no invitation to dinner or any other social event at a private house; but he appears frequently at balls. banquets, bazaars, and functions of a similar kind, when given by a public institution or in aid of a public charity.

A curious case of a ooctor's cleverness has just been toot we, and the anecdote is worth reproduc- ing. Some few years ago a country practitioner resolved to set up in London. He was undoubtedly versed in the knowledge of hi a craft, and had an excellent bedside manner. Moreover, his wife was I peculiarly charming person, whose singing espe- cially he hoped would carry him far where the cul- tivation of acquaintance was concerned. But he had one fatal drawback—his appearance was hope- lessly juvenile. However, after much cogitation,he resolved to rectify the defect by dyeing his hair white. The stratagem has proved a complete sue- .es, and the doctor in question now makes a most ltict ative income, though the snowy hue of his locks is now, alas quite natural. Whether Nelson's ship, the Foudrovant, is being broken up or not, it seems that we are not going to get her. Patriotism has been stingy over the &natter. The few hundreds sent to the Lord Mayor will be returned, "as circumstances have rendered public subscription impracticable," the chief cir- cumstance being that the people won't subscribe. Why did not some shrewd capitalist take advantage of the fuss made about the old ship to buy her and s..t her up as a maritime museum on the Thames— a lmission one shilling a head?

Aldworth, Lord Tennyson's Surrey home, is on the least frequented side of Haslemere, behind Black- down, the heathery highland which effectually separates it from the growing town. From its windows a magnificent view of widely stretching country is seen, country that is so little marred by modern landmarks that it might be a primeval plain rather than the very near neighbour of a fashionable artistic settlement. This, in effect, Haslemere is. But a few years ago scarcely known to the Lon- doner, a beautiful retreat in a beautiful part of Surrey, Haslemere is now quickly becoming Cock- ney, the prey of the speculative builder, and the desire of such as want to be thought literary or artistic.

div.head: WHERE THE WOMEN PROPOSE.
div.p: WHERE THE WOMEN PROPOSE.

In the Ukraine, Russia' the woman does all the courting. When she falls in love with a man, she goes to his house and informs him of the state of her feelings. If he reciprocates, all is well, and the !ormal marriage is duly arranged. If, however, he is unwilling, she remains there hoping to coax him to a better mind. The poor fellow cannot treat her with the least discourtesy, nor has he the consola- tion of being able to turn her out, as her friends in such a case would feel bound to avenge the insult. His remedy, therefore, if determined not to marry , her, is to leave his home and stay away as long as she is in it. On the Isthmus of Darien either s.ex can do the courting, with the natural result that almost everyone gets married. A similar practice to that in the Ukraine exists among the Zuni tribe of Indians. The woman does all the courting, and also controls the situation after marriage. To her belong all the children, and descent, including in- heritance, is also on her side. The same custom prevails among the Vigrees, a tribe in Cabul,and the Nairs of Malabar. Among the Garo race of Abssam, in North-East India, it is not only the privilege, hut even the duty of the girl there to speak first, any infringement of this rule being summarily and severely punished.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 8, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 8, 1892.
THE HOLE IN THE FOUR-POUND LOAF.

„ I can put a hole in a four-pound loaf.” Some folks —commonly those with plenty of money—like to be considered as having "delicate appetites." They affect to think a good, hearty appetite a very vulgar thing indeed. Oh dear, yes! So like a horse or a dog, you know. Quite out of character for persons of sensibility and position. From these people (chiefly women) the fashionable doctor extracts pockets full of guineas. The people Who make deep holes in four-pound loaves are a different lot. But even they sometimes lose their grip, and the big loaf is as safe from their attacks as Gibraltar from a boy's pop-gun. How does it happen? Well it's hard to tell. Often the victims couldn't tell themselves. But can they ever ,again wrestle with the four-pound loaf? Oh, yes, when they find out how to coax back that same vagabond appetite. Here's what one man says on the subject :7

[Cory.] "1, Dennis Gray, town Sergeant, Sprout Lane, Mul- Ungar, in the County of West Meath, Ireland, do solemnly and sincerely declare as follows : " In March, 1886, I fell into a low, weak state, and did not know what had overtaken me. At first I had a

bad taste in my mouth, and my mouth was covered with slime, the whites of my eyes were tinged yellow, I had no appetite, and after every morsel of food, how- ever simple, it lay like lead. I had terrible pain at the chest as if I had a heavy load pressing on me. I felt low, dull, and miserable, as if something was hanging over me. The pain at my chest and side:was very great, the wind rumbling round my sides, and so bad was this that I could not lie in bed. I got very little sleep, and night after night I rolled from one side of the bed to tlic ot..hr trying to get relief. but all to no purpose. So bad have I been that I had to wake my grand-daughter to make me a cup of tea in the middle of the night. I gradually lost flesh, and became weaker and weaker every day. My legs trembled and shook under me, and as I went about my duties I had to stop and rest in the street, fearing that I should fall down. Suffering in this manner I struggled on month after month, but in great agony. After a time I had to give up my work, and for a whole month lay in bed quite powerless and helpless. I lost all life and energy, and felt that I did not care what became of me, for life had become a burden. A doctor was called to see me, who gave me medicines, but I got no better. I was poulticed and blistered, and rubbed with embrocations ; nothing gave me more than temporary ease. My condition was now critical, for I had to be assisted in and out of bed, and all my friends and neighbours thought I could not recover. Everything that could be done was done for me. A lady friend from Glasgow attended upon me for three days and three nights, and stood over me expect- ing every breath would be my last. In June of last year (1890), feeling a little better, I walked up the street, and called in at Mr. Rogers' drug stores, and toot up a book

lying on his counter. I read in it a case similar to mine having been cured by a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I was so impressed with what I readthat I at once procured a bottle and commenced taking it. After I had taken half the contents of the bottle I felt easier, my food agreed with me, and I rested better, and I gradually gained strength, and by the time I had taken three bottles I was completely cured. All my friends and neighbours were astonished at my recovery, and asked what had wrought the cure. I told them all that Seigel's Syrup had saved my life after suffering over four years and being at death's door. Since taking the Syrup I have never ailed anything and can now eat anything, and can put a good hole in a four. pound loaf.' No kind of food comes amiss. I truly be- lieve that Seigel's Syrup has been the means of saving my life, and I wish others to know of the marvellous benefit I have received. I hereby give full permission to the proprietors of this medicine to publish this state- ment in any way that they may think proper.

"And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true. By virtue of the provi- sions of the Statutory Declaration Act, 1835 (5 and 6 William IV. c. 62). (Signed) "DENNIS GRAY." "Declared before me at Mullingar, in the County of Westmeath, on the third day of June, 1891, a Com_ missioner duly appointed for administering oaths for Her Majesty's High Court of Justice in Ireland, in and for the said County of Westmeath, and I know the de-
ponent.
"RICHARD BOOKER LEE, ,Tg43.1.?t " Commissioner."

This is the way Sergeant Gray got back his appetite, and a very cheap and certain way it is, as thousands in Great Britain can testify. The cost of three bottles of Seigel's Syrup is just nothing compared with lots of time and doctor's fees, for doctors must live and that, too, on the money obtained from their patients, whether the patients get well or not. It was Mother Seigel's happy fortune to discover a remedy as good for the pocket as ,1 it is for the stomach, the liver, and the blood. And in all the round earth nothing wins so many hard. fought battles against indigestion and dyspepsia as Seigel's Syrup does; and nothing does so much to reconcile us to our daily bread, and make simple food more nutritious and palatable than all the luxuries that were ever in- vented to sicken fools and enrich physicians. Therefore, when you feet —if you: ever do—as the sergeant felt, try the remedy that cured him, and you, too, will regain the appetite to make a big hole in the four-pound loaf. And when the appetite comes, may the loaf be on your table to satisfy it.

div.head: IS A KISS A " PERISHABLE " ?
div.p: IS A KISS A " PERISHABLE " ?

It was the prettiest little nest of a room, with one window that opened straight towards the sun- rise, and one all cool and shady, with maple boughs. There were all manner of pretty little femininities scattered about, and in addition, a photograph of a very roguish young gentleman. " And then,' continue Primrose, hiding her face on her visitor's shoulder," he—he—kissed me ! "Just as any sensible man weuld," the latter re- marked. " Mamma never lets me accept presents from gentlemen," she said ; "that is, anything substan- tial, you know. Flowers or candy or fruit —of course that's different; they're what I call perish- able goods. But books or jewellery, things of that kind—what I call staple goods—she never allows me to accept." "And a kiss you class among the perishables, I suppose, to be kept?" " No," said Primrose' demurely, " among the staples. I returned it."

div.head: WAS WELLINGTON SURPRISED?
div.p: WAS WELLINGTON SURPRISED?

The generally received notion that the Duke of Wellington was surprised rPceives confirma- tion in many pages of " Waterloo Letters," and perhaps most markedly in a letter from Sir William Napier, the historian. Napier gives the following account from the Duke's own mind] : " Ile found the Prince of Orange at the Duchess of Richmond's 1 ball on the evening of the 15th. He was surprised to see him, because he had placed him at Binche, an important outpost, for the purpose of observing and giving notice of the movements of the enemy. He went up to him and asked him if there was any news. • No, nothing but that the French have; crossed the Sambre and had a brush with the Prus- sian.. Have you heard of it?' This was news. So he told him quietly that he had better go back to his post-, and then by degrees he got the principal officers away from the ball, and sent them to their troops. This was done, 1 think he said, about eleven o'cloek. He then went to his quarters and found Muffling there, coming from Blucher with the news ; he ought to have arrived long before, but said the Duke to me, I cannot tell the world that Blucher picked the fattest man in his army tc ride with an express to me, and that be took thirty hcurs to go thirty miles."

div.head: ABOUT SMALLPDX.
div.p: ABOUT SMALLPDX.
BY J. D.

Warrington has since the 28th July, been suffer- ing from a visitation of smallpox. There have been altogether over 120 cases, out of which only seven sufferers have died. The fact is striking indeed, and furnishes ample testimony to the value of Sir William denner's great discovery. Those vac- cination marks borne by every sensible person on his arm have been as potent in warding off smallpox as any amulet of fabled virtue worn in the middle ages. Effectually shielded from harm by Jenner's discovery, we can form no adequate idea of the ravages which smallpox wrought in pre-vaccination days. In this connection, a few particulars respecting smallpox may not be uninteresting. According to the Chinese and Brahminical authorities, there is written evidence to show that smallpox has been established in their respective countries, during a period of three thousand years and upwards. Although smallpox had prevailed so long in China and Hindostan, the first notice of its appearance in Western Asia cannot be dated earlier than the middle of the sixth century, and Europe was not invaded until a considerably later pAriod. The occasion to which we allude, as the recorded com- mencement of its western ravages, was th 3 year 569, when the' city of M3cca, in Arabia, was be- sieged by an army of Abs)ssinian Christians, under the command of Abreha, with the expectation of being able to'clestroy the Kaaba or Pagan temple, contained within the city. In this army the small- pox committed dreadful havoc, and we are told that measles made its appearance at the same time. From the siege of Mecca, A.D. 596, to the siege of Alexandria, in the year 639, no Arabian records that have come down to us make mention of the progress of smallpox. The disease, however, during that in- terval was undoubtedly propagated in various directions in the wake of the victorious Arabs who were assembled and led forth to war under the ban- ner of their prophet. War has ever been a channel for the dissemination of pestilence, and, as Persia and Syria were shortly afterwards subjugated by the successors of Mohammed, we may fairly con- elude that smallpox was imported by the conquerors into those countries, if it had not already reached them.

On the other hand, Amron, the lieutenant of the Caliph Omar, invaded Egypt in 638, and two years afterward rcaptured Alexandria. It is conjectured that smallpox was communicated by the Mohammedan troops to the inhabitants of the city, during the siege. Ahron, an author, who lived in Alexandria at the time, wrote a treatise on small- pox, to which Rhazes, the famous Arabian physician, alludes, but the work has unfertunately since been lost. Smallpox probably reached these isles about the coin mencement of the ninth century ; but no distinct account of this extraordinary visitor is furnished by the writers of the time. Sunk in the ignerance of the middle ages, they allowed the worst scourge that ever thinned the human race, to pass withour description, or if mentioned at all in their meagre chronicles, it is only under the name of plague—or of consuming fire—epithets then applied to eruptive pestilences in common. Countries which have received smallpox in com- paratively modern times, afford striking examples of the magnitude of the calamity in its unmitigated terrors. In:1517 St. Domingo was infected. The island then contained, it is said, one million of: Indians, but those unfortunate people were alto- gether destroyed by smallpox, and the murderous arms of their Spanish invaders. About 1520, small- pox broke out in Cuba; thence it was carried to Mexico. Within a short period, according to com- putations that had been made, the pestilence des- troyed, in the kingdom of Mexico, three and a half millions of the inhabitants The Emperor, brother and successor to Montezuma, was amongst the victims. At subsequent periods, different parts of the American continent suffered much. Whole nations of warlike Indians were almost extirpated, and the piles of bones found under tufted trees in the interior of the country, have been supposed to bear testimony to the ravages of the dead malady. Peculiarities of climate exercise no mollifying influence over the violence of smallpox. Iceland was invaded in 1707, and it suffered as much as the southern regions. Sixteen thousand persons were destroyed—more than one-fourth of the estimated population of the island. Greenland escaped until 1733. In that year smallpox appeared and carried off nearly all the inhabitants. Smallpox is now familiar to every section of the globe, but wst hear of it no longer as a scourge which sweeps away the population of an extensive district with a rapidity and power approaching to those of a tornado. The beneficent providence, which for the fulfilment of its own mysterious purposes, tolerates the growth and extension of numerous plagues, has placed within the reach of human intelligence numerous remedies capable of either alleviating or of com- pletely obviating their dangerous effects. Inocula- tion has now, for many years, been wisely aban- doned by the medical profession, and vaccination is used in its stead.

div.head: WARRINGTON YOUNG MEN'S CHRIST [AN ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON YOUNG MEN'S CHRIST [AN ASSOCIATION.

A well-attended concert was held on Thursday week in the Sankey-at. Co-operative Hall, in aid of the funds of the y.M.C.A. From a musical point of view the concert was a great success, the pro- gramme,which was a varied and excellent one, being admirably rendered. During the interval, the Secretary (Mr. W. H. Bailey) read the report, which stated that the Committee had great pleasure in stating that the Young Men's Christian Association had, during the last year, made very satis- factory progress. The increased interest shown by all the members in taking up the different branches of work was a good sign, they thought, for the future welfare of the Association. They were very glad to be in a position for offering more advantages to young men now than at any other period since the Association was formed. The Committee called special attention to the highly competent teachers they had been able to secure for the various classes, which should guarantee success. I They were looking forward to the commencement of a Bible class or men's meeting on Sunday afternoons. On Monday evening Dr. T. Starkey Smith had kindly con- sented to take In hand an ambulance class. Special thanks were due to Dr. Smith for his valuable ser- vices, inasmuch as he was making no charge to the Association, and only a small charge was made to cover other expenses. The classes for shorthand would be held on Tuesday evenings, Mr. Brown being the teacher of these classes. On the same even- ing an elementary tonic sol-fa class and a tonic sol-fa select choir would be held, the teacher being the Rev. E. Moore. The committee had been able.to make special arrangements with the Warrington Gymna- sium for the members of the association. The Warrington Chess Club would also hold their meet- sings in one of their rooms, and members had favour- able facilities offered them for joining. The Debating Society, with their esteemed friend Mr. Florden as pre- sident,lwould meet every other Wednesday night. Mr. W. H. Butler had kindly taken up a class for the study which should prove most interesting, " Christ and Christianity.' aria those who entered the class had the opportunity of sitting for examination in April next, when prizes and certificates would be awarded to success- ful students. Every Thursday evening, until the Bth of April, there will be provided either concerts, social gatherings, or lectures. On Friday evening there is a prayer meetings for Christian workers, conducted by the general secretary. A conversational bible class is held specially to nein Sunday school teachers from all churches; the international Sunday school lessons would form the subject of discussion ; conductor, Mr. F. R. Roberts, M.A. Mr. Roberts would also conduct a class for the reading of the Greek text of the Gospel of St. John. Also on Friday evenings there would be a glee and choral society, conducted by Mr. C. H. Pigot, which it was hoped would be useful to the Association. Reference was also made to the Harriers, Draughts, Tennis, Cyclists',and Cricket Clubs in connection with the Asso- ciation. The Finance Club, it was added, would need further assisttnce from friends in order to avoid a deficit at the end of the year. Miss Bessie Dutton had intim- ated her regret that she was unable to be with them that evening. She wished him to say that the work in connection with the Y.W.C.A. would re-commence about the end of October, and she would be very pleased to enrol a few more rnembers,and also one or two volun- teer workers. . The programme, was, as we have said, was admir- ably rendered. It included instrumental performances, by Messrs. Pearson, Bond, and Payton; songs, " Biddy Aroo" and "Star of the desert," gr. Fieldhouse ; songs, "By the fountain" and " Thad O'Flynn," by Miss Jennie Jones; songs, " Dreams " and "A summer's night," Mrs. Pearson; Bono's, "The Arab's troth" and 'Mona," by Mr. R. W. Illakeley ; duet, "'The moon bath raised her lamp above," Messrs. Blakeley and Fieldhouse.

It was the amazed looks of the passers-by that caused him to stop and ask himself where he was going, what he was doing. At length a policeman stopped him, gently touching him on the arm, asking him if he were well.

" Well? Yes, lam well," he replied. "What do you mean?" "People are looking at you, sir. You are talking to yourself, and seem much excited." "Excited!" cried Arthur, with a wild laugh. "That is a tame word. lam mad I A woman has driven me mad! Then do not taunt me, do not seek to detain me, or I shall kill youll " He spoke so fiercely that the man started aside and let him pass. He looked after him, saying bo himself:

"He is quite right. If ever a man was mad, he Is the man." "Where are you going, sir? Have you not made a mistake?" said another voice. And 104- ing up, Arthur saw he had passed his hotel with- out knowing it, and the porter stood before him speaking. Arthur Rochester staggered forward, and the man stretched out his arm to save him from a fall, looking earnestly at him to see if it were wine or illness.

He, too, started back in wonder at the white, haggard face and wild eyes. "You are ill, sir," be said. "Do come in and let me fix you up a cordial." "Yes, I believe I am ill," replied Arthur, hoarsely. When he had drained the cordial which the man brought him something like life came back to him, although the haggard, ghastly look did not leave his face.

"Do not say anything about my illness," he said. "It is passing now, It was but a sudden, fierce pain in my heart. lam better." "You may be better," thought the porter, "but you look awfully ill." "I shall take the first train back to New York," he continued.

" You will have barely time, then, to catch it, air." said the porter. He had no time to spare, and he set about making his preparations at once. He had plenty of time for thought as the train whirled on to New York, and to lay out his plans for the future which was to be spent with lonie. "I will not give up to my sorrow—give way to It by recklessness and dissipation. I will show her that I am a man of too strong a will for that—and too brave. I will plunge into business, and by hard work seek to forget." Great was the surprise in Mr. Rochester's house- hold when Arthur returned home, and so soon. "What could have altered handsome, bonny Mr. Arthur, so in two *hort days?" the servants asked in wonder.
Arthur was thankful now that he had not spoken to his aunt and Elaine, his father's ward, about his approaching marriage to lonia, and that no one knew it save his father.

To him he simply stated that the affair was broken off. Gentlemen never discuss such matters together in detail, and although Mr. Rochester was much amazed, he asked no questions, accepting such information as his son chose to vouchsafe. Hs was secretly pleased, however, for again the hope sprang up in his heart that in time Arthur might learn to care for Elaine Granger. If they were to marry, the hope of his life would be realised.

He was too wise to make such a proposition ta Arthur a second time, and have it rejected. Arthur Rochester plunged heart and soul into the vortex of business, and in hard work sought solace for his woes. It was beneficial, as it gave him little time for thought or brooding. If occasionally a beautiful, wistful, girlish face, with clustering, nut-brown curls around it, and a ir of beautiful, appealing, dark, velvety eyes rose before his mental vision, he would banish it at once by working all the harder. If she could be happier with his rival than with himself, he must not complain, he told himself. "You are working yourself to death, Arthur,* Elaine told him one day. "You are growing quite pale and thin, and that will never do. "It does not matter much," he replied wearily. "But it does matter," persisted Elaine. • "It pains me to the heart to see you looking so pale and wearied." The sympathy of beautiful Elaine pleased him. Be bent his dark, handsome head over the little white hands, and kissed them in a chivalrous fashion. He was dismayed to see the whiteness that crept over the girl's face, followed the next in- stant by a burning flush. She drew her hands quickly from his clasp, and hurried out of the room without uttering a word. Indeed, she could not. Her heart was beating so tumultuousl3. "He is beginning to care for me at last," she mur- mured to herself, as she hurried to her own room. "At last the dream of my life may be realised. I would give my fortune—my very life almost—for his love. Oh, Arthur, Arthur, you will never know how much I care for you." That was the first intimation Arthur had that his father's ward was more than ordinarily inter- ested in him, and the knowledge troubled him. He tried to put the idea from him at first—tried to laugh at it, but it was in vain. The uncomfort- able conviction grew daily, yet there were times when he told himself that it must be only his fancy, simply that and nothing more. He was a gentleman, not a coxcomb. He was not so vain a man as to believe that every woman , who looked at him was in love with him. He told himself that he was doing Elaine an in- justice, attaching undue importance to her every word and action.

Still, many thins made him pause and think. She certainly evinced great preference for his society; she was never so happy as with him. She would give up any engagement—any promised', pleasure—to be with him. She consulted him on most things; she seemed to identify her interests with his. But all this might be the result of years of friendship, for she had been an inmate of her guardian's household since childhood. It might have nothing to do with love, vet it seemed very like it. He reproached himself for the thought; yet, dt what he would, he could not drive it away. The suspicion haunted him; it made him miserable. If it was really so, what was he to do? Another will take "If it gave her so much pleasure to be with him, the grief into his heart, and nourish it there, and why should he deny her that crumb of comfort 7 " die after lingering months. 1 He felt rather pleased and flattered, too, that one No one can mistake a tree blasted by lightning, young girl should love him so dearly, even though No other death leaves such traces. No one can lonie did not. mistake a flower struck by the terrible black Thus the winter passed away and spring came— blight. So no one can mistake the face of a man spring with its green, sloping hills peeping through whose heart is breaking. It may be cold, cruel, the fast melting snow. proud, stern, unbending, but the blast and the It had been four months since that memorable blight are there, day when lonie Lawrence and Arthur Rochester Arthur Rochester had dismissed the coupe, so he had parted, and yet he had not been able to forget was obliged to return to his hotel on foot. He was, her. By day and by night the sweet face was on the whole, rather glad of it, for it seemed before him, haunting him with its loveliness, and to him he would seek constant motion or he would always bringing with it the pain of bitter regret. go mad. i People in the streets who saw him moved quickly away from him. His white, set face and burning eyes startled them.

CuArrna XI. a STRANGE BETROTHAL. Matters might have gone on in this way for ever, had not a strange event happened. One day a long and important letter came for Mr. Rochester, informing him that valuable ore bad been found on a piece of land belonging to him in Europe, and strongly advising himself or son to come over at the earliest period and attend to the matter in person. ' "It will double our fortune, Arthur," said the old millionaire, rubbing his hands together gleefully. "Now it remains to be considered which of us had best go. lam not as young as I once was; I rather dread sea voyages." "I will go gladly, father," returned Arthur. "I should like it ahove all other things." The' matter was fully discussed at the tea-table, but one seated there turned pale as death as she listened. It was Elaine, but in the excitement no one looked at her, or noticed her emotion. , She turned to Arthur at last, asking, huskily: "If y 026 go, Arthur, how long shall you remain away 7 ' "As the song goes May be for years—and it may be for ever,'"

be answered, laughingly. Again there was the same pallor overspreading the gtrl's white face. He must have been blind not to have noticed it. "When shall you go ?" she asked, presently, and her voice sounded scarcely human in its sharp woe. till they did not notice that there was anything amiss. "The last of this week, I suppose," returned Arthur, absently. "It is short notice; still, affairs can be adjusted in time, I think; at least, I shall do my best to get oft." "Arthur is anxious to leave us," said his aunt, reproachfully. Elaine Grainger uttered no word. She could not. She rose quickly from the table and quitted the room. He did not know that she had reached the draw- ing-room, and, while passing through it, had fallen white and senseless to the floor, and there, soon after, Patrice, her maid, found her. It was quite half an hour afterward that Arthur Rochestel, while searching for a paper he had laid down somewhere the previous evening, remembered that he had left it in the drawing-room, and thither he went at once in search of it. He had pushed open the door noiselessly, and was just about .to draw the inner velvet portiere aside, when the sound of violent weeping fell upon his ear. Involuntarily he paused in wonder, and at that mo- ment he heard the sound of voices. He turned quickly away, but ere he could bake a single step he heard that which held him spell- bound—fairly rooted to the spot. It was Elaine who spoke, and her voice was freighted with sobs, and he realised that she was talking to her maid. "Patrice," she was crying wildly, "If he goes. I shall surely die. I could never lose him again." ".I shall begin to wish that .he had never come

hack, if you grieve after him in this fashion, Miss Elaine." Elaine only answered by a great cry. She sat by the window, her head laid on the window-sill, in the very abandonment of sorrow. Her lovely hair, all unfastened, lay like a veil around her; she was weeping sueh violent, passionate sobs that it seemed that each one must rend the girl's heart in twain. "Do come to your room, Miss Elaine," the girl urged; "there you can cry to your heart's content. Here some one might enter at any moment." But the girl turned away with a bitter cry. "He will go away and my heart will break, Patrice," she moaned. "And he will never know that it broke for :ove of him. Tell me how to bear it I shall turn my face to the wall and die. Before he has been gene one week, I shall be in my grave." "Oh, my bonnie young lady, do not say that," cried Patrice, in distress. "It is dreadful; it is not right. Indeed, it is not." "He has been the one love of my life ever since I can remember, Patrice," sobbed the girl, piteously. Other girls have had many loves; I have had only one. I repeat, life would be nothing to me without him. 06, Patrice, I know it is wicked; but I wish I could die in the hour Arthur bids me fare- well."

Those words brought Arthur Rochester back to the uncomfortable position he was placed in. He turned hastily away. He would not for the whole world that they should find him there. He went away as silently as he had entered, and hurried out into the street—to think—with a dazed, , bewildered confusion in his brain. Then the suspicion which had haunted him long ago, and whk h he had almost forgotten since, was quite true. Elaine loved him. Now that he knew it for a certainty, he was dis- mayed by the shock. Why, he had never looked , upon the girl with a lover's eyes at all. He had been most careful to give out the impression that he should never love, never wed. Yet he could not blame the girl for so pardonable a folly as loving himself. Arthur quitted the apartment hastily; but what he had heard still rang in his ears. Was there a man living who would not be proud of such a love —who would not be touched by it—the pure, deep, sweet love of a young girl's heart ? He was touched. He remembered his own grief and pain, his own torture and despair. How he had suffered to mad- ness because he had loved one who did not love him. And now glaine had the same pain to enders. He could not bear to think of it. Then, hurrying along the crowded streets, an Idea came to him—he could not tell how cc why Why not marry Elaine His life, so far as all its prospects were Can- verned, had enaed, for It was more than likely &mi. by this time, Innie, the girl whom he loved, was another man's wife. 'ln the wide world no one . cared for him except Elaine. Could he let Elaine die broken-hearted because she loved him? Mar- riage would bring him DO happiness, He did not look for it, did net. want it. He could not tell her frankly he had no love give her, that his h but if It wouldart was dead ; make her ly,ppy to spend her life with him, it should be so. T His wlolenhotaLrtr wldhsomul lia.l t le ec bieernioatilieicle.ofrom it emia he calli a wife? Could he hear to spy • kind words, to hold any revolted woman farnoymotth, heer w idea.o n He handh,,a innehviser? loNvoed except bole, and she alone could be his wife. But Elaine—poor Elaine who loved him so—what would become of her? f action not fully settled as yet. He He turned and walked hastily back to the house, hi-, course o anted more time to think of it. But the one thought recurred to him ever and anon. All hap- riness for him was over. If he could make Elaine ',;3l,py, why not marry her

div.head: UNFIT FOR HABITATION.
div.p: UNFIT FOR HABITATION.

In one congested area alone there were 184 houses con- demned, and these,numbered 32 to the acre. There were now in the town 500 houses which were under the ban of the Medical Officer. Who was t) blame for this state of things? Who blocked the way? He would tell them without hesitation. It was-- Alderman flanarsog : The Irish Question blocks the way. (Ladghter.) Councilor noon said that when these matters had been urged on the committee no one had opposed the reports of the medical officer but the chairman. He always said that be did not care for the opinions of the medical officer. He had opinions of his own. The Chairman had paralyzed the efforts of the committee in bringing about better things. He repudiated the state- ment of Alderman Sutton, that the members of the committee wished to shift Alderman Burgess. There was no clique in the committee. Councillor Dr. CANNELL asked the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee whether the committee had taken into consideration the necessity for closing the publit schools in the face of the continued increase of small-pox and scarlet fever? During his practice as a medic& man he knew of 40 cases at houses where the children were attending at sthool. Alderman CRAM= exitressed his regret at the.;

Alderman Sorrow was proceedmg to move the adjournment of the Council, as it wasthen nearly nine o'clock, when Councillor Iktatn; rose, and remarked'in an exciteable manner :It is monstrous. I moved mu amendment to the minutes, and here we are all sold, my amendment not having been 'submitted. I was told I should be allowed to submitit at a later period•of the meeting. f think this is monstrous work. The ratepayers are com- pletely robbed of their money. Connedlor Dixon, being allowed to proceed by the Mayor, moved that the resolu- tion relating to the appointment of Dr. Gornall's son to assist the Medical Officer for six months, at a salary of £l5O, be referred back to the committee for further con- sideration.
The MAYOR ZiArill anyone second the amendment? Councillor HILT, : I will do so.

Asked for the reason for the passing df the minute. Alderman BCT IMESS said Dr. Gornall had more work than he could possibly do, and it was absolutely neces- sary to give him assistance. It was tke opinion of the Medical Officer that they would net get rid of the epide- mic of smallpox.within six months. PSe did not intend to state that much, but he had done so.

Alderman HAMMON appealed to Councillor Dixon to withdraw his amendment. Councillor DIXOIc : lam not in the habit of withdraw- ing. (Laughter.) [wirautrr THE BA.SSINETTE.] ISY JOHN PEELLE. (Continued.) 'laving so satisfactorily rid the world of its super- fluous professionals and shown how it might get along very well without these—alas! to as unregen- , erates—necessary evils; having also, as in duty bound, found acoloay wherein to settle these mem- ben; of the three professions which society had out grown and so ceased to require; satisfactorily that is to ourselves, if not to other inhabitants of the said colony, who might not regard the incursion of these professional waifs as unmixed blessings in black cloth-; having, I say, so far and so well pro- vided for the welfare of posterity by ensuring them better health and fewer Drs.; less litigation, and fewer lawyers, and less superstition, and fewer parsons, we may now turn, with the grateful sense of a duty fulfilled, to our more immediate concerns. Set stay ! I cannot leave the matter in this state without hoping that these remarks of mine will not cause a panic among the ecclesiastic dignitaries of the Parliamentary Church ! It would be very sad to seethe market glutted by a rush upon them of fat church livings Or to see the business of a Bishop advertised fer sale, with all and sundry its goodwill. -stack anclatings, with a full account of the take and turn-over per annum! Without waiting to see the dffect of all this upon the price of advowsons, how would it be to try and reform our Parsons I We have reformed our funerals—or at least have been advised to dc, so—and our tailor's bills, and lotberunpleasant things, corn laws, and everything, in-fact—except ourselves—and this we leave for a grand coup, to The accomplished when we have leisure,and everything else has had its turn. So, why shouldn't the Parson have his innings. You needn't laugh, and cry ' Impossible !" The thing has been done. How? WIS, by making society better than the parson and rf,) shaming the parson into being better than himsel If.

Avery great deal has been done in this direction of late, and.much more may be done in the future. It has now ,come to be the nook that teaches the shepherd rather t ;han the shepherd teaching the flock. It is true ;hat there are a few backward learners who still i insist upon doctrines unsuited to the times; but it is patent to .all that a great improvement has t aken place inthis matter within living memory. And this improvement has been commensurate w ith, and consequent on, the advance of culture in their congregations. Where now be the Plutoni , sulphur-breathing cleric of our young days—whert now thecondemner of the span —long unbaptised t o eternal fire Society became too good for him ! The extinction of the untittest has improved him from off the •carth ! We have only to cast our eye t over—say Russia and some of the €tates of South I Ameriea—and compare their clergy with ours, duly taking into account also the several social con ditions to he convinced that Priest and parson a re alike very much the crea- tures of their enviro umente Wellanay we in Eng- land feel thankful t. hat we kave each a cultivated laitycnd that car ch trgy are to some extent amen- able by its influences. Any country with a separ- ately educated clergy has therein the germs of cor- ruption within itself. Monday morning to bind (me 4:gain, though alone, on Lavernock beach. More chiseliog and chipping, mote hammering and tapping, more Ostrea, more Porten and Lima, and, more than AR these—more characteristic fossils, among which was ifodiola minima. Here I had a whole stay—,cday splendid in its weather, and happy both in its pursuits and results; a day witkal— -of bard work if not of hard fare.; the latter consistil agof biecuits cod stale buns snatched as occasior offered front among the debris, the rooks and wrecks of 'former ages, at the bottom of my hand-bag. This 1 eaten fare was moistened by sparse sipping of the water thatilnipped from the face of the cliff.

My fast care, howel-er, reaclarag the shore was to snatch., by favour o-;,. the. sun and.aecamera, the kiounterfeit presentmact ot: the cliff and the beach —this while the liglit,•vas good. Seated Avon one of the oft-mentioned 'ledges of outcrop/slug lime- stone, regretting the loss of my chisel, -covered by the iticomiag tide ere licould recover it,i had leisure to marvel at the great ne.mbeir of beds lying in thin layers 0 IRV over the ottipir above my headrfor more than a hundred feet. Az each of these layers and beds nepresent the resultal subaqueous deposition, their ,quiak alternation .of character and fossil contents, teach us that here cosmic ,or local changes have affected the character of thediposi- tiam.

Here, an the limestone ilsand, we have what is neither more.ner less than ,a fossil graveyard; the band itself being mainly the result of marine .ar- genie deposits,, besides beingithe sarcophagus of the larger kind ofdossils. Here, ,too, we have bands af life and bands of .death ; tede representing favoatr- able and ohhers,unfavouratile .conditions affecting marine life. The limestone alepresents a time of clear seas—of vigorous prosperous life, when the molluea and the sarriane—the id-thy—and the pleai —married and gave in marriage, feasted, fattened, and thought not of .tgae morrow—basked and sported in the beams of a sun younger by aeons than this of ours—(which, as ,is well known, was turned off " ptomiscuous like",oue day among other small mat- ter as a subsidiary to this great globe of ours—to save gas and candles)younger then,laat whose hoar antiquity has near doubL'ed itself since then. And it, is, indeed, fascinatingly interesting to think that , here, in some measure,we may project e,ar thoughts into the middle period .of the world's history as laid open to us in the great stone book—Nature's epi- tome of the past. Curious also to inquire if cosmic show any sign of decadence now as compared with then, when old time himself—that is terrene time—was young. Nature is conservative of energy, and it is an inter- esting inquiry to ask of her as to the permanence of her forces ; was, for instance, the atmospheric pres- sure at M. S. L. then as now 15 pounds to the square inch 7 Was a drop of water (pure) of the same size then as now? Was the angle of incidence equal tothe angle of reflection; and had those early times their " rainbow at night "—to be " the shepherds delight "—ere yet there was an eye to see or a brain to poetize it into a promise of future good? All these questions may some day be within the grasp of science and receive proper solution; but these quiries are too many and too abstruse to expect a fellow to solve while sitting on a cold stone eating stale buns. Besides, dinner hour is gone and I must dig away and endeavour to fill that " beggarly account of empty boxes" which now offends the geologic eye by its blank hiatus in our otherwise excellent collection.

As this was my first day of working alone, and the tide rapidly rising and covering the scene of my investigations, I went at it with all the ardour of a sportsman to make a "bag." To a Warringtonian these beds are more particularly interesting because they are the complement to his own Tries. The reader who has given any attention to the matter, will know that our old town stands opcm what had used to be called the new red i•atuisbite-formatiot Now if this sandstone be traced southward through Hill Cliff—where in the quarry some of its great thickness may be seen—on through Stretton to the " wiehes "—the Mid-Cheshire district, where the now consolidated residuum of the Great Salt Lakes of those times form, the source of the mineral wealth of the district, here the red marls and flaggy sand stones of the Keuper—constituting the third term in our Trias—becomes the uppermost and eviden- formation. At Lymni, too, these flag stones had used to be got in the Windmill Quarry. On these flags were trequently seen the casts of the foot- prints of the Labyrintliodon and so called " ripple- marks " and sun-cracks. Even the pig-styes about Lymm were edged with these sPeeinlens—the desi- derata of many museums...

But fi-is—a-Tar cry from the Penarth Rho3tics and Keupers to Lymm and the" 'wichee." Stillthe gist of all this is that these many layered beds`j may be regarded as leaves absent from a book we.bare on our own shelves. They are as I have before said, the complement of our own Triasic series, wil;ch would be incomplete without them; this, and the fact of our representation of the Trims being almost absolutely unfoesiliferous, while these Rhcerics are full of the remaina-of old life, make these Penarth sections very interesting. Speaking of the apparently 'sudden change which seems to have taken piece

in the condition of the water—as evidenced by the nature of the diposits—one fact is very noticeable, viz., the associalion of a" bone-bed with the band of black gypsum and Ferric Sulphite in form of Iron Pyrites. The condition of this softer interlayer of the harder limestone—this indurated mud, whose upper surface is densely crowded with the black and shining fish scales, bones and teeth—indi- cates the occurrence of some catastrophe which wrought sudden destruction upon the finny folk. The fact of this being a superficial deposit on the bed precludes the idea of its being a continuous deposit under normal circumstances. The fossils enclosed in the bed—as distinguished from those laying an its surface—may be regarded as the result of deposition from deaths occurring under the ordinary quiet undisturbed conditions—but here, in the bone-bed they lie strewn in close contiguity, as though some sudden change in the water had killed off its inhabitants.. The close concomitance of the two sulphur com- pounds—a sulpate and a sulphite—with this bed of death, would seem to indicate on irruption of dui- phur in some form. A copious exhalation of sulphurous acid gas might account for the sudden. . destruction of life as shown by the condition of the bed. Anyway it seems to have been an abnormal ' and an unquiet deposition, as evinced by the dis- integrated state of the remains—entire skeletons beim; conspicuously absent. But now a declining sun warned me that Mon- day's work was nearly over—at least the collecting part of the day—and there was a rough tramp to the 'bus to face.

Next day I took steamer to Bristol on toe way to iitist Cliff. Now it has been said, by one who knew, that" tide and time wait for no man." Not only is this so, but the tide makes one get up sometimes very much ea: lier,than one would other- wise do—and as a compensation keeps us out of bed sometimes when we would fain be there. The " Marchioness" was timed to start at 7.45. It was not, .nuch more than 8.30 when she did it. Small blame to her, though for not doing it sooner Cardiff mud is very sticky and not conducive to speed when a vessel is in it. But the tardy tide came at last and after much backing and filling: warping and twisting we turned the awkward cor- ner and were away. . . . .

Our passenger; consisted mainly of navigators , and navvies, a few wheelmen with their machines, a few tramps like myself, a fair sprinkling of the fair sex, and last, but not least, two poor old horses. These two were, I believe, engaged on their last service—as they were on their last legs —that of carrying their own hides to the tanyard. They were tethered well forward in the foredeck—athwart snip—and bore their own and the added ills of the voyage, with most exem- plary patience. One was a large bay, lame on the off fore, which was bleeding, and wrapped in a piece of old sack. The other a little oldgrey—in which the proverbial straw aday had been attained, if not surpassed—so osseous and fleshless was he. This poor creature made the extremity of its distress manifesto's well as the in humanity of its keeper,by endeavouring to eat the wicker-work casing from some bottles near him. I carried the remembrance of this ill-used old servitor with me through the country lanes, with all their wealth of luxurious feeding for such as he, lying wasted and unused, on the roadsides. That man is surely a hard task- master who denies—for greed—so willing a servant the simple necessary of a whisp of hay. The state of the deck, at the end of the trip, was eloquent of the needs of these poor animals. So runs LLe world —plenty on one side, and direst distress on the other.

Shortly after leaving the harbour, our good ship turned her head more to the eastward, and thus encountered something of a beam-sea—resulting in a slight roll—which again resulted in the temporary retirement of some of the ladies, and also some of the more tickle stomached "gents." One young girl, however, greatly daring, braved the sight of her tormentor, and "in silent contemplation sad," leaned pale and pensive on the bulwarks. Now, of course, we were favoured with the prescnce of one of those bold and hardy spirits, who to hear themselves tell the tale, have before time bray ad all the perils Neptune could inflict The particular specimen under review—who had the look of being more used to skipping a counter than walking a deck--showed his manliness by standing before this pale and patient sufferer, and talking of fat pork and other (to sea-sick folk) nauseating viands. It is this kind of fellow who, when real oecatiiim for endurance does arise, is seen to creep into SOMe quiet corner and—well—has all the starch taken out of him. Surely "the law is a ham "that it preseute 118 kicking such boors. . .

But as we neared the mouth of the Avon, the seas wentdown and the laçhee recovered,and proclaimed themselves to be ma-eh better, thank you !" Into uhe winding Avon here mud bounded and there dis- playing magniffcent sections of rock high above our neads—Uadar the.fire suspension bridge at ulitton —touching at the lasi:ding stage where some cruel jokes wer.4 lined off at the expense of our hungry tour-footed fares—as that they were consigned to the Fresh Meat Sausage Company,and one remarked that for his part Ae should refrain from that form of diet for some time after this ! Si, only afterwards I landed for the first time in the ,4Vic.ilt: city of Bristol.
(To be routi'aued.)

div.head: CHURCH CONGRESS.
div.p: THE CHURCH CONGRESS.

EXTRAORDINARY SCENE. The Church Congress opened at Folkestone on Toes-- day. the members being welcomed by the Noncon- formists and by the Mayor and Corporation on behalf of the inhabitants. The Archbishop of Canterbury replied to these greetings. Processicns were formed to St. Mary's, Holy Trinity, and Christchurch Churches, but agaibst this a body of Low Churchmen practically pro- tested by displaying a banner representing Ridley and Latimer at the stake,and exhorting Churchmen to with- stand idolatry, priestcraft, ritualism, and Popish proces- - 8i011,9, They attempted to break up the procession, but the banner was seized and toru to shreds. Sermons were delivered at the churches named. On Wednesday the subject for discussion was " The neglect of religous instruction in elementary schools at • home, in the colonies, and in other countries." The Earl of Winchilsea read the first paper, and argued that it was the duty of the State to give religions instruction. In the afternoon the Congress discussed the duty of the Church to, the agricultural population, one of the most'- notable speeches being that of the Rev. Dr. Jessopp,. who urged the Church to take a more active interest in, the labourer, saying that as matters looked now the, cassock was by no means a match for the shirt sleeves, At the meeting in the Exhibition Theatre .discussiond took place on canon law in relation to church govern-- ment. A special Congress meeting heartily adopted a resolution against Welsh Disestablishment, The women's meeting, at which Mrs. Benson presided, was a most successful gathering. The hall was densely crowded, and the speeches were earnest. The industrial position of women, trade unionism, and co-operation were amonethe subjects dealt with. Lady Frederick Caven- dish spoke on temperance. Physical recreation and temperance were the subjects under consideration at the night meetings. The Church Congress resumed at Folkestone on Thursday. One section had an interesting discussion on poor-law administration. Outdoor relief was con- demned by many and defended by some, and the opponents and advocates of a State pension scheme were also heard. Another section debated the educa- tional, evidential, moral,: and devotional value of the 014 Testament for the Christian Church. It was resolved to hold the next year's congress at Bir- mingham, a cordial invitation having come from tha).. city.

PERHAPS the most notable of the National Songs. many notable volumes of the "Golden Treasury Series" pub- lished by Messrs. Ma cmillan and Co. is the one entitled "The Song Book." It is a compilation of "the best songs by deceased poets and musi- cians of Great Britain and Ireland." There is a guarantee that the work is well done when it is stated that the songs have been selected and arranged by Mr. Joetx HUILAH, Professor of Vocal Music in King's College, London. When, further, it is made clear that the volume includes the tunes as well as the words, that it is well printed,, neatly bound, and is to be had for half-a-- crown, it will be sufficient, we should think, to set people wondering how so much that is good can be ioffered for so little money. It should be explained that,. although the tunes are given, the songs are presented without accompaniments, tau object being to submit them in their original forms. It is the tunes, as a matter of fact, and not the accompaniments, which have come down to us from olden times. What is of spacial interest, alike to the musician and the student of literature, la to compare and contrast the merits of these fittest of survivals. There is such a. thing, to be sure, as a disenterment of that which the world would have willingly let die; but this is not by any means characteristic of the present collec- tion. On the contrary,there is evidence.en almost every page of some phrase or couplet that may be said to have become a part of folk-speelithrough- out the kingdom. Who is there that does not at times find some of these phrases Tanning in his.; head" without being able to Damember thein source? We have found it very pleasant to. stumble across some of these gems in their origi- nal setting; and it will be the same, we cannot but think, with other readers who devote a few hours to this unique Song Book. One writer has aptly remarked that music and sweet poetry agree, As needs they must—the sister and the brother. In all the old songs that have kept their popu- larity, there is usually this happy agreement, though such is the power of a noble tune, that it is capable of keeping alive ignoble verso. In some cases, we have what seems mere nonsense jingle, as in—

The frog would a-wooing ride, Humble dum, humble dam, Sword and buckler by his aide, Tweedle, tweedle, twine. Shakesrare follows the same custom It was a lover and his lass, With s hey, with a ho, with a hey none:go. The modern refrain is doubtless the outcome of this practice, and, properly used, it is a great improvement upon • it. " Come live with me and be my love," supposed to be written by Marlowe,. is quite free from any oddity of style, and is very pretty pastoral. There is perhaps no liner oftener quoted than "In the merry month of May," and it is therefore of interest to note that- I the song is taken, as well as " Come, sweet lass from "Pills to purge Melancholy," The line, varied to "All in the merry month of May," occurs too in "Barbara Allen "—a most popular ballad at one time, and more than once referred to by GOLDSMITH. Here is a verse from" Harvest :Home " which, as kicking against tithes, is , scarcely likely to be selected for singing at, current ; harvest festivals : We've cheated the parson, well cheat him, again. Why should the vicar have one in ten r One in ten ; one in ten ; Why should the vicar have one in ten ?' }hex JONSON'S "Drink to me only with thine eyes" is of another class. Music and poetry are of the highest order, and the song is therefbre likely to continue a favourite with future as with past generations. "The Roast Beef of old land " also belongs to the same period, both words and music being by RICHARD LEVERIDGR. A Re ACCORDING to the ancient adage— volt When thieves fall out honest men In camp. get their own;,, and in a similar Way it may be said that when Councillors quarrel ttls ratepayers get at the truth. There is a "a very pretty," but a very fierce quarrel between the Chairman and the members of the Sanitary Committee of the Warrington .aorporation ; and there was some very plain and 40rae very rough speaking at the meeting, on Tuesdly night, of the Town Council. It has been 4PParent for some time that the majority of the embers of the Sanitary Committee were restive

tnder the autocratic management of Alderman ttuauEss, the Chairman. It has been a common %raark that they were ciphers, and that he was the only unit; but the ciphers have revolted; the krures refuse any longer to work as they are wire- Polled by the Chairman. Assuming that half ealy of what was said on Tuesday night is true, they ought to have revolted years ago; and have %red the town from the result of the gross

; aegligence and mismanagement from which it ia at present so seriously suffering—both in Pocket and in health. But "better late than never," if they will only go through with what they have begun. According to their own show- " it is impossible for the Sanitary Committee, as at present constituted, to do its work ;" and, as that work is of the highest importance—in view of the epidemic 9f scarlet fever and of smallpox, which are scourging the town— it is imperative ; that immediate steps be taken to remedy a state ' of things which is as discreditable as it is lament- able. The only rational way out of the difficulty i 3 for the Chairman to retire. He has no confi- dence in the Committee, and the Committee have 1:1° confidence in him. Baside=i, he has, on two t'ecasions within the past three months had his Proposals rejected by the Council as a whole. It may be said the Council should let the Corn- raittee " fight it out amongst themselves ; but the issues are too grave for such a course. The Council cannot thus shirk its responsibility as the governing authority ; arid the over-burdened rate- Payers have a right to look to the Council for relief. Judging from the admissions made by the embers of the Committee, things are about as had as they can be. Councillor Greening tells us that the Longford Sub-Committee have " found the Machinery in a very deplorable condition; " and Councillor H. ROBERTS affirms that the Said-
tarY Committee have acted " with regard to the

lirEtall-pox epidemic like a lot of old women." They have been sitting with their hands tied behind their backs ; and "he did not hesitate to say, and it was the opinion of 99 people out of every hund- ted in Warrington, that if they had provided for the first 20 or 30 cases of small-pox the Chances were ten to one that the out- break would never have reached its pre- sent dimensions." Councillor BEAMAN stated that 'through the mistakes of the past—they had been told by Alderman Bu RGESS in that Council Cham- ber that tha most ignominious failures had been the most unqualified successes." Councillor FLOOD followed this up by alleging that when matters affecting the condition of the town had been ul'ged on the committee" no one had opposed the reports of the medical officer but the chairman Ile always said that he did not care for the' opinions of the medical officer. He had opinions 1:4 his own. The Chairman had paralyzed the efforts of the committee in bringing about better things," Councillor BONNELL, another member of the Committee, had his tale to tell ; and it was that he himself" advised the conversion of the tlaybridge iron works into a hospital three weeks before the epidemic gained large propor- tions. Alderman BURGESS said he could not Ilee his way to adopt the reccommendation." And Yet the recommendation was adopted when "too !4•te!" If the Haybridge works had been turned 'llto a hospital at first instead of at last, there is every reason to believe that small-pox wciild by this have been stamped out. How long has this Reign of Misgovernment to continue? Alder- -111, an BURGESS blocks the way; and the block must removed. Further, the Sanitary Committee gas too much to do; it should be divided into two Committees—one to ma nage Longford Works, C. ; and another to see to sanitary matters generally. It is in this way that the Augean stable is to be cleansed ; and it is for the Town Council to show itself equal to the operation.

Great poets have generally written something at one time or another which may be taken as a more or less accurate descriptive of themselves. Tennyson was no exception in t his respect, for in "Queen Mary" we find the following lines, which have reference in the play to old Sir Thomas Wyatt : Courtier of many courts, he loved the more His own grey towers, plain life, and lettered peace, To read and rhyme in solitary fields, The lark above, the nightingale below, And answer them in song.

The Rector of Warrington, in the "Parish Church Magazine," strongly urges upon parents the desirability of giving, as a free donation to the school funds, the pence which under the Elemen- tary Education Act are now being saved to the parents. But it is natural to ask, "Where is the advantage of Assisted, not to say Free Education, if what is saved in school fees is to be given as a contribution to the Schools?"

The fact is the old system of taking school pence is better than this now plan, for fees were collected from all alike, whereas this giving of surplus pence will mean that,while some contribute all they can, others will give nothing at all. We sympathize with the Rector and other school managers in the difficulty in which they find themselves, and would suggest that" the way out" is not by vol- untary gifts of school fees, but by establishing a School Board.

Warrington is one of the very few towns of over 50,000 inhabitants that have not established a School Board; and the circumstance is spoken of in some quarters as something to be proud of. We think, on the contrary, it shows lack of perception of the signs of the times. The most go-a-head towns and cities in the country are those in which the School Board system has been longest at work. They can, under a Board, provide Higher Grade Schools, at a fee not exceeding ninepence, where an education of the very best kind is given. In Warrington, scores of children are leaving school every year, simply because they have passed the ordinary standards. In a Higher Grade School, they would continue in training ; and they and the town would nenefit by it, while the annual cost to the ratepayers woithi certainly be less than half of a year's loss at Longford Works.

The Church Congress at Folkestone, on Tuesday, seems to have been pretty lively in its opening proceedings. The processions of the High Church party were denounced by their brethren of the Low Church as idolatrous and Popish. More than that they sought— To prove their doctrines orthodox By apostolic blows and knocks.

An attempt was made to break up a procession, by a body of Churchmen, who flourished a banner with a picture on it of Ridley and Latimer; but the attempt failed. The banner soon ceased to flourish, for it was seized and torn ; and Ridley and Latimer were compelled, so to speak, to bite the dust. Thrice happy Church that isso "broad" as to embrace " high " and "low," and provide such a " variety entertainment," on the shortest notice.

One of the tricks of trade amongst tramps is to go about with a child or two, and then appeal for sympathy. It is not very difficult to make a child look miserable under such circumstances, and then, of course, the coppers come in all the more freely. But there are "coppers" (police) of another kind, and one of these latter has been the means, at Southport, of a tramp of 60 being sent to gaol for a month for exposing his child in order to obtain alms. It was found that the girl—nine years of age—was lame through walking forty miles in a pair of boots four sizes too large for her. It would never have done to wear an old pair of the right size; the big boots were "fetching." The old sinner actually had the impudence to plead that he would be unable to obtain alms if the child were taken from him.

The evidence accumulates that the McKinley Tarift was passed not in the interests of the people of the United States, but of the managers of rings and syndicates. Like all such protection, it is a case of plundering the many to enrich the few. The tariff on tinplates, which has so disor- ganised trade in this country, has been worked, curiously enough, to advance a rival industry. The "Pall Mall Gazette" says : As to the origin of the tariff,the same Congress- man has declared that the increased rate of taxes oh tinplates was lobbied through Congress largely by what is known as the American Corrugated Roofing Company. That company desired to place so heavy a tax upon tinplates, thus increasing their cost to American consumers, that a tin roof would cost more than one made of corrugated iron. The till roof was a competing product. They desired to tax it out of existence, in order the, they might have the field without a rival. They succeeded, and that is the industry which is flourishing, and not the tinplate manufacture."

DEATH OF AN OLD RUNCORNIAN. On Tuesday morning an old Runcornian passed away lin the person of Mr. John Stubbs, ot 29, Regent-street, Runcorn, at the age of 74 years. The statement of accounts showed a balance in hand of £24 4s. 7d. The ketiring members Mrs. Speakman, Mrs. Fisher, and Mrs. Fieston were re-elected and Mrs. Fred Norman was elected in the place of Mrs. Marwood who had left the town.—Mr. S. Tay- lor was re-elected treasurer. A committee was appointed to arrange an entertainment in aid of the fund.

Cte t. PRITCHARIVB for the best ire guinea wateh a work- ingman eau Lave.—Advt. ST. Jonw's CHOIR, RUNCORN. On Tuesday last the choir of St. John's Presbyterian Chapel, with friends, numbering together about 50, spent a social evening, which proved to be of a most enjoyable character. The proceedings commenced at 6.15 p.m., with an excellent sandwich tea, prepared by Mr. F. Jones, assisted by the lady members. Then followed a very interesting and profitable meeting, over which the pastor,the rev. J. Pulford Williams, presided, and he delivered a short but appropriate address. Mr. Charleston sang in good style "The boys of the Old Brigade," followed by a duet, very tastefully rendered by Mesdames Burn and Warburton, after which Miss S. P. Hayes rendered " De banks of de ole Tennessee " in her usual clear and effective manner. The quartet" If God be for us" by Mesdames Richardson and Burn, and Messrs. Warburton and James Richardson, was very nicely sung, and was followed by Mr. Arthur Robinson, who made his debut by singing "The Rose of Sharon" in a very promising manner. Mr. W. G. Jackson evoked much laughter by reciting in his characteristic style " The Village Choir." " The Jubilee Selections " by Mesdames Richardson, Timperley, Warburton, and Burn, Misses S. P. Hayes, and Warburton, and Messrs. Charleston, A. Robinson, James Richardson, and Warburton, accompanied by fuegulo, violin, and guitars, was an unusual item, and gave evidence of careful preparation, being rendered in a very creditable manner. Mr. E. Worrall, who was in good voice, sang "When other lips" in his usual excellent style, and Mr. James Richardson, rendered in a fitting manner "I'll tell them to be true." rhe duet by Mr. and Mrs. Burn. entitled " God shed His Light from Heaven," was well interpreted and much appreciated, and Mrs. Temperiey , was quite at home in her rendering of "There is a flower that bloometh," which she sang well. Then the song entitled " The four jolly smiths "was ably sung by Mr. Leathwood (Halton) and Mr. Warburton rendered in his usual earnest style " The Harbour Bell." The pianoforte and guitar accompanists were Mrs. Burn, Miss Warburton, and Mr. James Richardson.
