div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 8, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 8, 1892.
RUNCORN BOWLERS AT BLACKPOOL.

There has been concluded at Blackpool this week, the great autumn bowling handicap which attracts bowlers from all parts of the country. Mr. Robert Wright, of Runcorn, a well known bowler, was very successful. He won five games, nesting such men as T. Meadows, H. Baines, W. Marlcinson, W. Talbot (champion of Eng- land) and Schofield. He was eventually beaten by Eli Yares. Tom Woods, another local bowler, managed to survive the third round. Jostle, PRITCHARD-$:1 sale shop is 51,Hign-st., nis workshop 4, lirid.-st„—Advt. WIDNES CYCLE CLOD. On Thursday evening the distribution of prizes in con- nection with the abeve club took place at Ow Conserva- tive Out -room. Dancing, &c., was a fterwards indulged in until early morning. The following is a list of prize winners :-25 mile race, handicap 7 Ist, David Dalgleish, gold medal ; 2nd, Frederick Sherratt, gold medal; 2nd, Walter Sherratt, silver medal, gold centre ; 4th, Walter Norris. silver medal.. Five miles championship ; let, David Dalgleish, silver cup, pre- sented by Mr. Robert Turton, and gold medal ; 2nd, Walter Norris, gold medal ; 3rd, Walter Sherratt, silver medal, gold centre. One lap slow racelast man in wins first prize : let, Thomas Coupe, order on Widnes trades- man to the value of 12s. 6d. ; 2nd, Fred Franklin, order for 7s. 6d. ; 3rd, Tom Jones, order for ss. PRITCSIARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- aad 4, Bridge et., Buicorn.—Advt,
AN EAGLE AT RAINFORD.

A gentleman residing at Rainford states that on Saturday, an eagle, which would probably measure six feet across the wings. was seen near that town, and had apparently come from North Wales. It hovered about some time, and then went in the direction of Birchly and Garwood, and, it is be- lieved, settled in a wood. .Severel gentlemen went out to shoot.it if possible, but no information of the result is to hand.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED,—I. RIO W. DITI'TON, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Adv. BURTONWOOD SCHOOL BOAHD.

The adjourned meeting of the above Board was held in the class room, Burtonwc.od, on Tuesday, when there were present Messrs. James Warburton ichaitman), John Warburton (vice-chairman), Thos. Norcott. Thomas Perks, Wm. Fairclough, John Fors- ter (attendance officer), B. Gawthorpe (scho3l master), Wm. Webster, (clerk). The minutes of the previous meeting were read and confirmed. The correspondence of the month was considered, and the clerk directed to reply to same. The clerk re- ported the receipt of the quarterly instalment of the fee grant .£l9, and the same was ordered to be debited in the cash book. The application of the Technical Ethication Committee for the use of the schools for classes in needlework, ambulance and nursing, drawing, arithmetic, and mathematics, to be held on Tuesday and Friday evenings were con- sidered and granted, the price to be charged to be decided next meeting. It was resolved that the parents of several irregular scholars be summoned, and that the time of meeting during the winter be 12.30 (noon) instead of 7.0 p.m.
HOT WATER FiTTER.—GARLAND, Ironmonger, Warrlngtoll; Bratich—Earlestown.—ildv. PRESENTATION.

On Saturday evening several of the members of the choir and congregation, together with the churchwardens of St. Peters Church, Newton, met in the schoolroom, for the purpose of presenting Mr. Peter Fairclough, organist of St. Peters's Church, and Miss M. A. Grace, a member of the choir, with a handsome marble timepiece and a purse of gold, on the occasion of their forthcoming marriage. The Rev. F. W. Johnson (curate) in the unavoidable absence of the Rev, LI. Monk, presided. Dr. J. W. Watkins in making the presentation • referred to the long connection of the parties with St. Peter's Church, Mr. P. Fairclough, as organist for about 20 years, and Miss Grace as a member of the choir. The timepiece bore the in- scription—" Presented to Mr. and Mrs. Peter Fair- dough, on the occasion of their marriage, by the clergy, choir, and congregation of Newton-le- Willows, October 3rd, 1892." Mr. Stuart (church- warden) on behalf of the officials of the church, in a felicitous speech, then presented Mr. Fairclough and Miss Grace with .a purse of gold. Mr. Fair- dough thanked those present in . a very hearty manner, for their kindness and forethought towards himself and his future wife. Miss Grace also briefly returned thanks.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankepat., Warrington.—Adv. THE SAD DEATH OF A Boy AT ST. HELENS.

At the Town Hall, on Saturday, Mr. Brighouse held an inquest on the body of Harry Fowler, aged ten years son of Mr. Francis Fowler, plumber and painter, 338. Kensington, Liverpool, who was killed on the London and North-Western Railway, at Carr Mill Viaduct, on Wednesday. It appeared from the evidence that Mr. Fowler had a contract with Messrs. R. and J. Rankin, of Birkenhead, for paint- ing the ironwork of the new widening of the via- duct, and he had taken his lad to stay in St. Helens with him for the week. On the day named the lad was with him at work, and during the dinner hour went with apprentices into the wood to gather blackberries. The father had his dinner under the bridge, and on going to the top again he saw his boy picked up by a platelayer named Williams. was unconscious, and died the same night in the Providence Hospital. Williams said he saw the lad run across in front of the train, and shouted to him twice, but lie went on. Witness was thirty yards away, and could not help him. Richard Haitian, the engine driver, said just before came to the bridge a ballast train passed. lie was coming fifteen or twenty miles an hour, having slackened when he saw the flagman. The stoker said "Hold, mate, a boy has run in front," and witness whistled. He then saw a boy in a stuoping position, and be thought he had fallen over the wires. He went on to St. Helens, and reported the occurrence to Foreman Porter Wilding. A juryman asked witness why he did not atop, and he replied that he did not think the lad had been struck, and if he had stopped on the viaduct, which was 601 t. high, passengets might have alighted, and have fallen over. tie thought the lad had crossed at the back of the ballast train, and did not see the pas- senger train.. He must have been struck by the buffer.—The father said he did not blame anyone, and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH.

On Thursday, William Henry Watson, of 10, Cookson-st., Blackpool, who had come to lodge with his sister. Mrs. Rodgers, at 144, Duke-st., St. Helens, started at the Hardshaw Brook Chemical Works of the United Alkali Union, and after being at work 20 minutes was found leaning over his barrow quite dead. Ile appeared to have been a healthy man, and his sister was not aware that he suffered from heart disease, if that was the cause of death. Jos RPH PRITCHARD keeps spectacles to suit all sights from a shilling a palr.—Adtit.

BOWLING MATCH AT RUNCORN. On Thursday, a bowling match was played on the green attached to the Bridge Hotel, Runcorn between Thomas Wood, a local man, and James Rothwell, of West Leigh, for £lO3 a side. There was a large attendance of spectators. The green, was not in first class condition, owing to the recent heavy rains. The betting was 6 to 4on the visi- tor. From the start until 20 was reached, the game was of an even character, the figures standing, Woods 20, Rothwell 19. After that the visitor drew ahead, the game called being Rothwell3l, Woods 23; 45, 34; 56, 46; 65, ; and 71, 61, the stranger thus running out the winner by 10 points. • If yea want a luck 7 wedding ring go to 51, litart-s.r.,where you will get a present with it.—Advt. A WIDNES FARMER AND HIS At Widnes County Court yesterday before Judge Shand and a special jury, William Grace, farmer, Upton, near Widnes, sued the London and North Western Railway Co., for damage in loss of a horse. Mr. Swift, barrister, appeared for tile plaintiff, and Mr. F. M. Preston represented the defendant com- pany. It appeared that the hor-e had been pur- chased in Ireland, and it was alleged that it was injured in ttansit by the Rid l way Company. The animal died three weeks later in consequence of the injuries it had sustained. After witnesses had been heard, Mr. Preston contended that it, bud not been proved, that there was negligence., on the part of the Company. The jury found a verdict tor the plaintiff on the ground that the Company had not exercised reasonable care in tying the horse. His Honour gave judgment accordingly with £45 damages. I-lousy:ll,lLn LINENS hemmed and maraed free of e'Pqrge.— J. and W. Durrost, Sansey-st. Warrington.—Advt.

THE MANAGEMENT OF rUBLIC-HOUSES. At St. Helens Police Court on Wednesday, before Mr. Sinclair and Mr. Walmsley-Cotham, Mr. J. 0. Swift applied on behalf of William Glover for a temporary authority until the 12th of December of the license held by John Smith in respect of the White Lion, tierard Bridge. It was stated during the hearing of the case that the applicant had managed one of Messrs. Walker's public-houses. One of Messrs. Walker's rules was that employes were not allowed to taste liquors during business hours. Applicant was ill one ilay and took a glass of beer. He was not dismissed for drunkenness, but suspended for breaking the rule. He would not go back, but started driving for Mr. M. G. Dixon. The White Lion belonged to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co.—The magistrates granted the application. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED. —J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington. —Ade.

WATIGRAVE CHURCIE. The Rev. J. Carson, took up his ministerial duties, as Rector, of Newton-le-Willows., at Wargrave Church on Sunday. At the morning service the choir sang the anthem "Behold how good and joy- ful a thing it is brethren to dwell together in unity.". The solo was given by Mr. G. Wright and .eiss M. E. Laithwaite and .-Miss G. Edwards sang the duet. On ascending the pulpit, the Rev. J. Carson referred to the words of the anthem, which he said reminded him of the duties that he had the, day entered upon. Ile spoke of the changes wLich had taken place, in connection with that church and hoped that he as pastor, and the congregation as parishioners, would work together amicably during the time he was spared to labour amongst them. The rev. gent lemeu then proceeded to read the 39 articles of religidn to which he formally assented.
TORTOISE STOVES, GARLAND.—lrOnrnonger, ~Vettritigtoll and Barlestown,—Adv.
DEgIiII:TION OF AN..ILLRGITIVATE CHILD AT

11 IDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr H. Wale-Deacon (chairman) and Lieut.-Colonel Gaskell, a single young woman named Alice Drury, residing at 10. Sunkey-st., was charged under war- rant with neglecting her illegitimate child on July 27th., Mr. Wood, relieving officer, said prisoner left her illegitimate child at her father's house in Sanke3-st. without arranging for its support. De- fendant's father refused to maintain the child, and it was removed to the workhouse, where it now is. The cost so far to the union was £3 14s. 6d. He was authorised by the Guardians to prosecute, and directed to ask for a conviction. Is answer to the magistrates' cl et k, witnese said he believed prisoner was going to be married shortly to a man named Cross. Prisoner was committed to gaol for a fort- night.

PETROLEUM STOvE.4.—GARLAND, Bridge-street. Warring- ton.—Ads. THE HOME IRON TRADE. The English iron market shows little change, although in several districts signs of genera lira- provement are manifested. There is, however, more activity noticeable in the ste,l-rail trade, and an order for 30,000 to 40,000 tons of rails and ac- cessories has been secured by the Ebbw Vale Steel, Iron,!and Coal Company. The Glasgow warrant market is firmer, and Scotch makers' iron is in fairly active enquiry. In Cleveland pig-iron is depressed. The ironmasters' returns for Septem- ber show an increase in stocks of 7,161 tons. The production is large, 216,848 tons, of which nearly half is hematite iron. The total stocks on hand are 53,269 tons, including warrants. There are 90 furnaces blowing, the highest number this year, 50 being on Cleveland iron and 40 on other kinds. , Trade in the north-west of England continues dull in both crude and finished iron. In manufactured iron increased orders are reported from the Midland district, and enhanced prices are secured ; but gen- erally the demand in this branch is limited, and in Scotland bar-iron is ss. lower. Little alteration is noted in the steel trade. In shipbuilding and en- gineering matters continue quiet. The coal trade is fairly steady.—lron.
HousKnoLn LINENS hemmed And marked free of charge.— Land W. DUTTON, Sank ey-st., Warrington.—Advt THE NEW POLICE COURT MISSIONARY.

At the Warrington borough police court on Mon- day, the magisti at es' clerk, Mr. H. B. White, intro- duced to them Mr. Henry Taylor, late of Derby, , where he had been secretary to the Midland Rail- way Company Temperance Union, and had now been appointed a missionary in connection with the Warrington police court. Mr. White read a letter from Mr. J. Hurst, of Liverpool, diocesan secretary, of the Church of England Police Court and Prison Gate Association, addressed to the Chief Constable, hoping they would find him useful in the office to which he was appointed, and assuring him that he would have no cause to regret the agpointment. Mr. White said there was a previous letter asking that Mr. Taylor might have a place found for him in the court, convenient for him to bear the cases so that be might deal with them at the proper time. Mr. Hunt had suggested that Mr. Taylor should have a seat on the right ot the magistrates' clerk, where be had been accomodated accordingly, and now be duly recognised in the capacity in which he had been appointed. Mr. Taylor has been appointed police court missionary for three districts, Warring- ton, Newton, and Widnes. Ile has visited a consid- erable number of men and women who have been before the court during the week.
When in want of a chaste and elegant wedding or birthday present go to PRITCHARD'S, 51, If igh-st.--ilcfct.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday, Mr. J. Pritchard presiding, and there were present the Rev. Canon Maitland-Wood. the Rev. Dr. GsAaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. T. Hand- ley, Salkeld, G. Moss (clerk). SCHOOL ATIENDANCE.-A YEAR'S WORK.

The School Attendance Committee reported that 50 parents had been summoned before them, and 43 appeared. It was ordered that 17 be prosecuted before the r. aaistrates. In several cases of irregular atten- dance of girls it was alleged they had been refused admission at the schools. There seemed to be some ; truth in this as the visitors explained that all the girls' ' schools were overcrowded, and the teachers were there- fore compelled to refuse admission. The Committee recommended the Hoard to consider the provision of further school accommodation for the girls in Runcorn, it a subsequent meeting of the Committee, the visitors' reports for the month ending September 30th were read. The average attendance was 3,001 as against 3,030 in the corresponding month of last year. The falling off in regularity was shown to be mainly in the Infants' schools. The annual report for the year ending September 29th, was read and adopted. The report stated 3,577 warning notices had been served by the visitors, against 2,849 last year: parents before the committee, 691, compared was 689 in 1891 ; prosecutions before the magistrates 376, against 125 ; average number on rolls 3,611, against 1,448 in .1891 ; average attendance, 2,958, compared with 2,768 ; percentage of attendance 81.9, against 80.3. It would be observed that during the year the committee had made increased use of its powers and this had been I attended with an inprovement in the attendance, the percentage on rolls having increased by 1.6. Leaving canal boat children out of the calculation, the percen- tage for the year would be 83, which compared very favourably with other towns. The children on the rolls showed an increase of 163. This was about twice the ordinary annual growth. The overplus might probably be accounted for by increased employment on the Ship ' Canal Works, and by the greater readiness of parents to send their children to school at a very early age, now that fees were either reduced or abolished. It might be noted that the percentage of attendance for boys was 86.4, girls 79, and infants 78.3 During the year two boys fiad been sent to the Bishop Brown Industrial School at Stockport. Dr. Gastaldi moved the adoption of the report, and said the-Committee had been rather strict in order to secure a good attendance. Still they had to congratu- late themselves upon having adopted such strict measures towards those parents who were constantly appearing before the Committee for the same transgression of being indifferent in reference to sending their children to school, because the results had justified the Committee in that course, and he thought the Board would continue on these lines. The people dealt with had been such as no law could bind to duty, except through a penalty. Mr. Salkeld seconded the motion. The Chairman said they were indebted to the energetic labours of the Atten- dance Committee, for the very much higher results. Dr. Gastaldi had been a very faithful and energetic Chair- man in this important department of the Board's work. As to the want of accomodation for girls, this was an important matter, bet the Committee did not state the numbers who could not obtain admission, or the num- ber it would be wise to provide for. He moved that the subject be referred to the Board at a future meeting. Dr. McDougall said there was at present a large floating accomodation in the town' probably 400 or 500 house- holders, most of whom had families, and it would be rather unfortunate to provide extra accomodation which would not be necessary afterwards. Before any attempt was made to deal with this question accurate Informa- tion should be obtained. The Clerk said he would endeavour to obtain the information necessary for a special meeting.—Mr. Handley said the Inspector had called their attention to the want of accomodation at Greenway-road School ; and they knew there was this want of accomodation ; could not they make temporary provision, if they thought the population would go down when the Ship Canal was finished? There were schools which could be hired no doubt.—The Chairman's motion was seconded by Dr. Gastaldi and carried.

PENNY SAVINGS BANKS. The Clerk reported with regard to the Penny Savings Banks in connection with the Board Schools, that there were at Green way-rd. Boys' Schooll66 depositors, whose savings amounted to £9 Hs. 2d. In the Girls' School there were 131 depositors and the amount to their credit was £lO 10s. id. At Mill Brow School there were 67 depositors,and the amount to their credit was £3 ss. sd.

div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. F. Wiswall the Chairman, pre- sided, and there were preNent NleNsrs. J. Dobson, D. Bisbrown, E. W. Humphreys, W. Leach, W. Hankin- son, T. Lee, H. Coward, W. Fisher, S. Taylor, J. Pritchard, R. Abel, J. W. Lightburn, Dr. Mangan, J. Meadowcroft, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (sec.), Dr. McDougall (medical officer), M. Barker (surveyor).

MICDICAL OFFICSIVS, REPORT. The Medical Officer reported that during September there were 37 deaths' of which one was'an inquest case. Of the remaining 38deaths 5 were due to convulsions. 2 to paralysis, 2 pneumonia,. 2 pthisis, 4 enteric lever, 3 mesenteric disease, 3 diarrhcee. and 3 to senile decay. The 37 deaths showed a death rate of 22 2, and, exclusive of the inquest case, of 21.8 per 1,000 of the estimated population._

div.head: TYPHOID FEVER CUTBREAK.
div.p: THE TYPHOID FEVER CUTBREAK.

Mr. Dobson desired the doctor to state how many Cases of typhoid fever there were in the town at the present time. If they had an enemy amongst them, let them know, so that they might cope with it.—Mr. His- brown desired to ask the same question. He thought they ought to have an authoritative statement from the Medical Officer.—Dr. McDougall stated that if the disease was ever of an epidemic character it was gradually sub- siding, and there were very few cases. (Hear, hear.) The matter was under investigation.—Mr. Humphreys asked if there was any reason why they should not have the inform ation.—Dr. McDougall said he had not got the exact number, but it could be obtained froin the regis- ter.—The Chairman said they could only deal with the report at present, and it they wished reference to be made to the register, it could be done at a later period.—At a subsequent period Mr. Light- burn moved the adoption of the minutes of the Health Committee, which contained several recommendations. With regard to private nuisances, Mr. Dobson said he was not a member of the Health Committee, and for the information of the public he wished to ask a question or two. Was it correct that an eminent doctor in the town reported a case of a young man suffering frem typhcid fever, in Mersey-street, being allowed to remain surrounded with all unfavourable circumstances for his convalescence, and with all the conveniences for the spread of the disease in a crowded thoroughfare ? The statement made was that an order was given to their Inspector for the removal of the patient to the Hospital immediately, but it was found days later that the case had not been removed. The Inspector, he understood, said he could not move the case, because of the inability of the people to pay 4s. per week, and thus allowed the man to remain, with the probability of the spread of the disease. Then was it true that the Hospital grounds were in such an unsatis- factory state as had been described? Two years ago it was put in a proper condition, but at the present, he thought it was a thorough disgrace to the Board, and an insult to men of intelligence. He thought it was quite time that something was done to remedy matters. Further, was it true that the internal arrangements were not satisfactory ? There was not a flower, not a picture, or anything to make matters cheerful about the place ; there was nothing to inspire the patients with courage and hope, or anything calculated to make them convalescent. He thought they ought to deal with the subject firmly and fear- lessly, and if there was anything wrong to remedy it. Mr. Lightburn said with regard to the case in question they ought to have something like accurate information. The facts had been based upop some communication which, perhaps, unwittingly the Health Committee had to a certain extent ignored, as it was not thought of sufficient importance to be 'sent direct, and it was not dignified for them to take notice of it. So far as remov- ing the patient was concerned, he might state thst he was away from home when the occurrence happened, and c•mseQuently was not cognisant of the fact. Before he went he told the Nuisance Inspector, in the presence of the Chairman, and if there were any cases with re- spect to which it was questionable as to the payment of the usual charge, they should be removed to the hospital irrespective of the cost, that matter being left for subse- quent consideration. So far as the hospital was concerned there was a Committee dealing with the whole question. They acted as a humane body, but at the same time . . with justice to the pockets of the ratepayers. Mr. Lea asked if there wag a resolution on the books 1 with reference to the removal of cases to the hospital and the consideration of the payment of costs after- wards. Mr. Lightburn not think there was. The Chair- man explained that it was understood that the Chair- man of the Heath Committee had power to deal with pressing cases, and he was present when Mr. Lightburn gave instructions for the removal of the cases at once, without consideration of costs. Mr. Lightburn said the costs ought to be spread over the whole Union. Mr. Leach asked if it w.re compulsory on the Board to remove those cases. The Law Clerk said it was optional to a certain extent. He thought there was a misunder- standing about the removal of those cases. It was not within the option of the officers to remove them, nor was it in the power of a medical man just because he gave an order that they should be removed to the hospital. it depended upon the patient himself, or, if an infant, on the consent of its parents. It was only when they were without proper accommodation, and when it was stated that the person was suffering from an infectious disease, that they could obtain a magisterial order for his removal. The compulsary taking to the hospital was when such an order had been given. In the case in question, when a magisterial order could have been given, the young man was too ill to be removed. —Mr. Lightburn asked if a letter tiad not been received from the Local Government Board with reference to the outbreak.—The Secretary answered that a commuuica- Lion had been received asking for a special report with reference to typhoid fever. The doctor had seen it, and they had had a conversation respecting it.—Mr. Light- burn said they must have the report and relieve them- selves of the responsibility.—The minutes af the Health Committee were then confirmed.—On reaching the general business, Mr. Meadowcroft said if Dr. McDougall did not send his report at an early date he should feel bound to give notice that at the next meeting they should appoint a committee to go fully into the matter. He did not see any reference in the minutes of the Health Committee as to the appointment of a sub-committee to deal with the hospital.—The Law Clerk explained that these matters were Rot inserted in the minutes until the report of the sub-committee was received.—Mr. Leach said that as one present at the committee meeting, he might explain that such a committee was appointed. Mr. Humphreys desired to know the number of infec- tious diseases, or at least those ot typhoid. The Secre- tary stated that the typhoid fever cases, including continued fever reported from September let to the present date, or for five weeks, had been 45. Mr. Humphreys gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that such information be incorporated in the monthly report of the medical officer of health in future. Time Secretary then read the letter from the Local Government Board in reference to typhoid fever, asking for a report. Mr. Humphreys moved that the Medical Officer be requested to report to the Board at the earliest possible moment, in accordance with the request of the Local Government Board. Mr. Bisbrown seconded the proposition, which was carried.

div.head: LIGHTING OF NEW STREETS.
div.p: THE LIGHTING OF NEW STREETS.

Mr. Flatillinson stated that it was not the fault of the Commissioners that the gas mains in certain streets had not been laid. He understood that the Gas Company intended to proceed rapidly with the work. They had promised to do it within a certain time, which had elapsed. He sugc>ested that the Secretary write to the Gas Company pressing them to complete the work. •

_ . . PROPOSED LIFEBOAT SATURDAY. The Parliamentary Committee reported that they had considered the letter of the Manchester and Salford "Lifeboat Saturday " Committee, urging the establish- ment of a " Lifeboat Saturday "in the district. Being unable to spend public monies on this object, but being impressed with the importance of the movement, the Committee recommended that the Chairman of the Board be asked to convene a town's meeting in his official capacity with the view of establishing a " Life- boat Saturday." Mr. Humphreys moved the adoption of the minutes. Mr. Taylor seconded. Mr. Meadow- croft drew attention to the fact that already there was an agency in the town to obtain contributions for so deserving an object. The Chairman said the present proposal was not intended to oppose any other effort. He expressed his intention to call a town's meeting for the purpose, so that they might assist those already engaged in the noble cause.

THE PROPOSED TECHNICAL INSTITUTE-. The Technical Instruction Committee recommended that application be made to the Department of Science and Art for a grant in aid of the building of a school science and art ; that the block plan prepared by V,r. Bowden, showing the land to be appropriated for the purpose of the Technical Institute, be adopted—con cents of plot 904 square yards.—The Chairman move': j, and Mr. Abel seconded the confirmation of the mir Mr. Pritchard thought the large scheme unnecet ,saty and uncalled for. They could not show by the ref, for technical education that the building w' as required with such numerous class-rooms as the one pt. °posed t be erected. There was no doubt that t b uirements a Science and Art Committee had ample accommodr Aion just now. They had made no representation to thr A Board that the

work in any way suffered for want of accommodation. With the exception of cookery and dressmaking, the teaching was conducted in two rooms. In his opinion they had ample accommodation, for there were rooms erected at the expenses of the ratepayers unused during the evening, and therefore the members should see clearly why they were called upon to duplicate those rooms in capital cost and maintenance. Were they justified in entertaining the elaborate scheme with the amount of resources they had available for the purpose? They had for technical education a sum equivalent to £4OO in round figures. If they were to have an institu- tion costing £4,000 there would be a necessity to mort- gage the penny rate for a long series of years, and theu there would be the maintenance of the building, so that possibly they might not have available for techni- cal instruction more than £2OO, whilst actually they spending more than that sum under existing circum- stances. Now, if the £2OO were expended in the two class-rooms, where there was ample accommodation, considering their available resources, he wished the com- mittee to show the Board how they would be justified in erecting a building having 13 class-rooms to maintain. He was aware in addition to that the scheme provided for a large room to be devoted to secondary education. He argued that that Board bad no authority whatever to engage certificated teachers to conduct secondary educa- tion, neither had the authority any fund by which they could contribute one penny towards that object. In his opinion the present project was an ill-considered scheme, and if it were carried into effect it might be that the ratepayerewould point the finger of scorn to it, and call it the Technical Institute Committee's folly. The School Board rate was about sd. in the S, the Free Library rate id., and the Technical Instruction rate Id., so that they were now receiving an educational rate of 7d. in thee. Under the circumstances he moved that the matter be referred back to the committee for further consideration. Mt. Taylor regretted that Mr. Pritchard should try to put a block in the way of one of the most beneficial institutions Runcorn was ever likely to possess. He took a different view of the subject in every respect. So far as the fund for the erection went, they expected that they would get something like £l,OOO, or more, from the Science and Art Department. Then they had a grant promised by the County Council of something like £5OO. Besides that, gentlemen who were favourable to the pro- ject had made most liberal offers, and he felt assured trom what he knew of Runcorn people, and their generosity, that they would be able to raise the fund for the Institute. Whit regard to the carrying on of the work, they were already in possession of about £420 a year, and he felt sure that to carry on the work, even if the 13 classrooms were occupied day by day, they would have a sufficient sum at command. It had taken them two years to get so far, and be trusted nothing would occur to delay the matter. At one time they ran a risk that the Board School would not be available for the object, and even now they had nowhere to put the models or anything else they possessed. A portion of the models were packed up, and there was danger daily of those in the Board School being injured. It was well known that they were only making use of the present accommodation until they got a room of their own. Mr. Humphreys felt himself in a difficulty. Be should be the last man to stand in the way of technical instruc- tion, but after the information given by Mr. Pritchard, he thought they were entitled to more particulars. It was a personal disappointment to him that they had not been able to do more than had been accomplished at the expense of about £220 per annum. There was every probability that under Mr. Acland intermediate educa- tion would be given for England, and therefore perhaps it would be well to pause before spending a large sum on a building. He seconded the amendment.—Mr. Meadowcroft had some sympathy with both sides on that question. He should be sorry to see that they were going backward in the furtherance of technical instruc- tion, but he thought they shculd not launch themselves Into a too extensive scheme, and any inquiry that would give information to the Board and show them how to act would be of value.—Mr. Lightburn asked if they paseed the recommendation would they be compelled to build the institution.—The Chairman: Certainly net.— Mr. Lightbnin said they had got a certain scheme before them, which would amply meet the requirements of Runcorn, and they had to consider h iv, to carry it out. They desired to know what the Science and Art Depart- ment were prepared to give them, and when they had got the full information they would be able to ascertain how they were to maintain the building. The resolution pledged them to nothing. With regard to the land ad- jacent to the Board School, it had been stated that it would be required for an infant school. He asked if the wonderful edifice, with its numerous class rooms, should be erected, would the cost be anything more than at pre- sent? He contended not. Therefore if it was to be an honour and credit to the place without costing the rate- payers one penny, what was the use of blocking it ? The Chairman said the resolution did not commit them to the erection of the institution, and it was a wasteof time to discuss the question of the institute, its maintenance, its cost, &c., at present. He was very sorry that Mr. Pritchard took every opportunity, with a carefully prepared speech, to drag in his pet scheme.— Mr. Pritchard thought that a very unfair remark for the Chairman to make. He had never mentioned the site. —The Chairman reiterated that Mr. Pritchard never lost an opportunity of raising his pet subject, which caused a great waste of the time of the Board. He did not see why he should object to such an expression. It was true—it was his scheme. The committee's project was not so black as it was made to appear. The resolution committed them in no way to the erectien of the Insti- tute, and there would be ample opportunities in future of discussing the subject.—Mr. Pritchard said Mr. Tay- lor had reflected upon the School Board by the statement he had made. There was never any doubt as to the School Board lending their rooms for technical instruc- tion.—Mr. Taylor said the question was raised as to whether the School Board should undertake the work of technical instruction. He fancied he could see as far through a stone wall as any one present, and he thought there was something behind it, and he gave a hint that if the ratepayers were deprived of the use of those , schools, those who advocated it would have to answer for their conduct. It did not get to that.—Mr. Prit- chard said he must correct Mr. Taylor on one point. The question was considered whether the School Board should carry on the schools, or allow the Technical Com- mittee of that Board to do the work, but the question of I withdrawing the use of the rooms for technical instruc- tion was never once hinted at at the Board meeting. If Mr. Taylor had get that idea he must have imagined it. —The vote was then taken, when five voted for the amendment and eight for the original motion, which was carried. The members who voted for the amend- ment were Messrs. Pritchard, Fiumphrey-s, Leach, Fisher. laud Dobson. IRRECOVERABLE ARREARS.

Id. be allowed; that the general district rate made on the 21st April last be amended by raising and reducing certain assess- ments as set forth in schedules to be submitted ; and that the consent of the Local Government Board be obtained to the spreading of the cost of the steam road roller over a period of ten years. div.head: ASSAULTS ON WIDNES POLICEMEN.
div.p: ASSAULTS ON WIDNES POLICEMEN.
EXENIPLARY SENTENCES.

Before Mr. H. W. Deacon and Leintenant Colonel Gaskell at Widnes Police Court, on Monday? a young man named Richard Rose, of no fixed abode, was charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the licensed premises of the Railway and . Commercial Hotel, Victoria-road,on Saturday night; there were three other informations charging bun with assaulting and resisting Police Sergeant Carter, Police Constable Crenshaw, and Police Constable Cochrane. About half-past nine the police were brought into the hotel, and ejected the prisoner, and on the way to the Police Station, he became very violent, and kicked the three officers about the head and face. The assistance of several civilians was obtained to take the prison ei to. the Police Station de pleaded guilty to assaulting Police Constables Crenshaw and Cochrane, but not guilty to the other two charges. For refusing to quit,. prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days, and for the assaults on the officers, he was committed to goat for 30 days, without the option of fines. John Appleton-St., was brought up on a charge of drunken- ness, and also of assaulting Police Constables Moseley and Bamford)? on Saturday night. The officers were taking the prisoner into custody on the first charge, when ho became very violent, and kicked both cull— stabls in a very brutal manner. Numerous previous convictions were proved against the prisoner, and he mwsitsted to gaolfo . and 4dlcodsatsys withfort an he drunkenness, d corn.. hard labour f.zr each as-. sault on the police.

div.head: WIDNES STABBING CASE.
div.p: THE WIDNES STABBING CASE.

At the Wit-Ines, Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. H. Wat4,B-Heacon and Lieutenant-Cal. Go.skell, an elderly man, named Isaac Houghton, employed as a war .erman, was brought up on remand, charged with v;ounding Walter Dyson, also a waterman, by stabbi mg him in the left side with a knife.—Prosecutor star/ A that about 630 on Friday evening he was near the be' ics on the canal bank, when he asked the prisoner hit flat had grounded in the Dee. Houghton did not • reply, so witness walked on. Prisoner followed and caught hold of him, when a scuffle ensued, and both men fell t 4 the ground. They were separated,and when witness went on to his flat his mate discovered that he, was bleeding. On taking his shirt off he found he had been stabbed.—Frank Cookson, a flatinan, said he saw Vele two men scuffling on the ground. Prisoner had a, large double-bladed clasped knife in his hand similar to the one produced.—Dr. WCambridge said he examined Dyson on the night in question, and found a wound one inch and a half long over the seventh rib, penetrating to the bone. It was a bad wound, and must have been caused by a heavy blow with a sharp instrument, which would have entered the lung but for the rib bone, Prim soner was committed for trial at the Sessions,

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
INSANITARY WORKSHOPS.-COBWEBS IN A CURIOUS PLACE.

At the Warrington BorCa-i-gl7l Police Court, on Monday, Mr. Norman, inspector of Nuisances, prosecuted Wm. Fiddler, fustian cutter, residing in 3, Hale-st., Winwick- road, for having his place of business in Oliver-st., in an insanitary condition, contrary to the Factory Act, 1878. Mr. Norman said he visited the place in July and found it in a very dirty condition, and on September 28th he found it again in the same state. There were cob- webs all over the ceiling, and the floors had never been swept or washA.—The defendant, who pleaded not guilty, was fined 20s. and costs, £1 9s. in all.—Mr. Monks, who presided said in face of the present epidemic of scarlet fever and smallpox, it was incumbent on occupiers of worships to keep them in a healthy condition. The defendant had no business to ask anybody to come to work for him unless he provided a healthy place to work in.—William Hargreaves, baker, residing at 6, Oliver-st., was then charged by Mr. Norman with a similar offence on the 28th ult. The Inspector said the premises complained of were a bakehouse behind the defendant's residence. He found them on the date in question in a very dirty condition. A sack on the floor was quite embedded in filth. There were cobwebs growing up th.e kneading troughs. He pointed these out to him particularly, and told him that places where the preparation of food was going on ought to be scrupulously clean. The defen- dant was fined 10s. and costs. A BIG MANURE NUISANCE. At the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednesday, William Burton was charged by Ralph Norman, as In- spector of Nuisancas to the Warrington Corporation, with non-compliance with a notice to abate a nuisance caused by the deposit of manure on the south side of the Sankey canal.—Mr. Browne represented the defen- dent, and said the action was taken under a peculiar section which gave one local authority the power to take coguisanze of a nuisance committed in the district of an adjoining local authority. He should like to ex- plain the cause of the alleged nuisance—for he did not admit there was a nuisance. Mr. Burton was a manure merchant and bought a large quantity at Liverpool, bringing it up by boats to the wharf on the Sankey Canal. The farmers had been working as well as they could to get in their corn, but as soon as they got it in, all the farmers to whom the manure, 700 tons, had been sold had been working at it to get it away. —Air. Browne consented to an order for the abatement of the nuisance within 28 days and payment of costs by his client.
JUVENILE ED

At the Warrington county sessions, on Wednesday morning, William Smith and James Murray, boys, were charged with breaking, on the 28th of September, into the house of James Dale, Sankey Bridges, and stealing therefrom a jacket, a pair of trousers, and an apron, value in all, 20s. The prosecutor's wife deposed that she left the house about three o'clock on the afternoon of the 28th ult., and, on her return at half past five, found that the door had been forced open, and the articles stolen.—Emma Swinton, employed at Tunstall's, pawn- brokers, Winwick-road, deposed to Smith pawning the articles there, as things they had been sent with, in the name of John Smith, for 3s. 81—Sergeant Devlin, of Sankey Bridges, said he apprehended the prisoners on the 30th ult. They admitted the offence, Smith said Murray had part of the money, and Murray that smith broke open the door.—They both now pleaded guilty.—The court missionary, in reply to the Bench, said he had visited the homes of the boys. He was sorry that the society he represented could not make,available any Home for boys at present, though they had one for men. He had written to the diocesan secretary about the lads.—The prisoners wets sentenced to ten days' imprisonment, to be followed by five years M a reforma- tory.

div.head: MINOR CASES,
div.p: MINOR CASES,
SATURDAY.— Before Alderman Burgess (chairman), Alderman Chandley, Mr. John Geddes, and Mr. L.

Voisey. AN EXCITED Parsoxsa.—Martin Connolly was charged on remand with being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st., on Thursday night. The prisoner was re- manded on Friday morning on account of his excitable and disorderly conduct in court.—Prisoner alleged that the officer was telling untruths. He grew very excited, and denied that he was disorderly. Whenever he came into the town he was always apprehended.—The Bench committed him to gaol for 14 days with hard labour. ANOTHER DRUNICARD.—James Heyes was, on the evid- ence of P.C. Jones,fined ss. and costs,or seven days with hard labour, for drunkenness and disorderly conduct at Bridge-foot, on Friday night. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall, Alder- snen Francomb, Sutton, Harrison, and Wright, and

Mr. F. Monks. DRITELENNESS.—Bridget Dolan, in Irlam-st., on Satur- day night, ss. ; Jessie Dixon, a Scotchwoman, at Bridge Foot, the same night. was discharged on promising to leave the town.—Thomas Craghan, in Buttermarket-st., at 12.5 on Sunday morning, ss.—Mary Jane Hamblett, a 'girl, was charged with being drunk and disorderly an Pinner's Brow, on the 24th ult. Mr. Taylor, the court missionary, obtained permission to take her in hand, and she was dismissed on promising to attend to what he had to say, and left in his hands.—John Urea and Michael Walsh, in Mersey-st., on the 24th ult., ss. and costs each. —Sarah Crookes, in Tanner's Lane, on the 25th ult. ss. —James Sankey, in Mersey-st. on Saturday night, es. ASSAULTING A CONSTARLE.2John Shields was charged with assaulting P.C. Amson, at a quarter to 12, on Saturday night, in Dial-st. P.C. Amson said he heard a woman say to Shields in Dial Court, " You scamp if a policeman was here I would have you locked up," and witness said" What's the matter ? "a ad she complained that the man had insulted her." The defendant on his speaking to him about the matter, struck him and blackened his eye. A struggle took place, and he man- aged to get away.—A month's hard labour. UNSEEMLY BEffeviorre.—Alice Thomas, 3, Naylor-st., 18th appearance, and Wm. Scott, 5, Jackson's-yard, were charged with this behaviour in Cockhedge-lane, on Sunday night.—Scott was fined 10s., and Thosnas was ordered to leave tha town at once. TnErrs FROM THE MARKET.—Arthur Longshaw, was charged with stealing on Saturday night, a pair of boots, value 4s. 6d., the property of Joseph Priestley, from a lock-up shop in the Market. He was also charged with stealing, the same night, from a stall tnere' three men's shirts, the property of John Peacock. He had un- hooked the boots, carried them about seven yards, and then threw them into a corner, and then came back as if to take them away. He was then given into custody. The prisoner denied touching the boots. The shirts were missed and afterwards found by Sergeant Cheney, when he apprehended him on the charge of stealing the boots. He stated that he found the shirts.—He was sent to jail for three months with hard labour. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE.—Thomas Brislam, shopkeeper, of Frudstam, and Joseph Schofield, black- smith, of the same place, were charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart at five minutes to twelve on Saturday night. They had half a bottleful of gin with them.—A publican was called in their favour, and said one of them was sober, and the other merry at a qUarter to twelve, on their calling at his house for some meal for the horse. He supplied them both with some rink.—They were fined ss, and costs each. 'DISORDERLY WOMEN.—EIIen Terry, Bridget RFoone, find Sate McDonald, three women, were charged with asorderly conduct in Buckley-st., on the afternoon of

the 23rd ult.—A police constable said the whole street was in an uproar on the occasion, and all were under the influence of drink. They had broken the lock off the door of a woman named Brady, who had been up at the court against them,and were throwing stones. The row continued for hours.—Mrs. Brady and an old man gave evidence. The defendants called a female witness, who said Mrs. Brady threw a big paving stone out of her window, and hit Mrs. Perry, and she threw it back and broke the windows. Brady also threw a bottle.—The defendants were each bound over for six months, and ' had to pay ss. costs each. Don CASES.—George Molyneux, forgeman, 20 Forshaw- street, for having his dog at large without muzzle or collar on, was dismissed, but charged 4s. Bd, for three days' maintenance of the dog in the police station.— Frederick Morgan, 77 Lovely-lane, for a like offence,and for not having a license for his dog, was fined 2s. Bd. and costs in each case.
TOESDAY.—Befcrte Messrs. E. J. Guest (chairman) and W. Owen.

_ DRUNK AND DIBORDHRLY.--Samtlel Perry, in Mersey- at., the previous night, 55., including costs.—James Edmunds, in Scotland-road, on the 6th of August, 10s. and costs.—Michael Farren and Martin Kelly were fined, the former ss. and costs, and the latter 55., for a like off ente _

A DISREPUTABLE WomAx.—Mary O'Reilly,for unseemly behaviour in Eaton's-yard, that morning, and for having been previously convicted of a like offence, and as to whom the magistrates conferred with the Court mission- ary, was sent to jail fora month.

WEDNESDAT.—Before Mr. John Fairlclough (chairman), Alderman Wright. and Mr. E. M. Crosfield. Dausk AND DISOUDERLY.—Catherine Doherty and Mary E. Smith were charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Tanner's-lane, also with breaking the door and window of Eliza Brady, the previous afternoon. P.C. 30 said the defendants were creating a disturbance and using very bad language. He took them into custody, and Doherty lay down, and would not go to the station. He got another constable to assist him to take her.— Inspector Bowen said the defendants were continually annoying people and necessitating police being kept there.—Eliza Brady said one of the defendants broke her door, and the other her window. They had pre- viously threatened her.—Smith said she broke both the door and window.—The Chief Constable said the neigh- bourhood of Erwood and Portland streets, which are off Tanner's-lane, were becoming unbearable. The police would prefer these characters to live in the same neigh- bourhood, so that they could put on strength, and deal with them, but really this place was becoming insuffer- able. Between Tanner's-lane and Gee-street, the police were fully employed. The witness Brady was in the box on Monday, and gave evidence against the sister of one of the defendants. It was fearful that neighbour- hood.—The defendants were sent to prison for a month, and another month for the damage.—Peter Murphy. drunk and disorderly, in Bridge-street, on Tuesday night, was fined ss.—Thomas Kelly was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Market Gate, and assaulting William Morris, a cripple, on Tuesday night, 103. and costs.—John Rowland, drunk and disorderly, the same night, in Bank-street, was fined ss.—Joseph Massey, in Mersey-street, ss. Tawnsner.—Before Aldermen Chandler (chairman) and
Sutton, and Captain Ridgway. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Annie Harrison, in Bridge- st., the previous afternoon, was discharged on promising to leave the tswn.

BEGGlNG.—Catherine Brown, for begging in Manches- ter-road, on Wednesday night, was fined ss. and costs. VAGRANCY.—John McHugh and John McKay were charged with being found sleeping at Dail= Forge that morning, and having no visible means of subsistence.— The constable employed at the works stated that they had opened the furnace door and pulled the fire out to have it around them.—They were sent to jail for seven days each. BREACHES OF THE EDIICATION ACT.—Joseph Frangleton, file forger, Smith-st., Samuel Hiles, file cutter, Bank Quay, Mary Ellen Holden,laundress, Beswick-st.,George Povey, boiler maker, Buckley-st., Thomas Robinson, tanner, Mersey-view, Mary Towey, Oliver-at., whose mother, Mr. Riley said, had spat in his face the last time he spoke to her about her child, William Thompson, forgeman, Buckley's-court, and Wm. Williams,forgeman, Guardian-st., whose lad was threatened with the birch rod if his father was summoned again. FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison (chairman), and
Fiancomb.

IN UNLAWFUL Possessi-o-x-Fa-t-rick Connolly, labourer, was charged, that he, being a convicted thief ,was found in unlawful possession of two hay-forks. He was remanded till Tuesday. FRAUDULENT Exusirmewr.—John Ford, labourer, was charged with making a false answer on attestation on enlistment in the 4th battalion, Liverpool militia, by stating that he had not been discharged from the army. —The defendant denied his guilt, but was sent to prison for a month.

TREFTS.—Thomas Davey, forgeman, Dallam-lane, was charged with stealing boots, on Tuesday night, from the shop of Joseph Bakehall, 112 Bridge-st.—The prose- chtor deposed to missing the boots about half-past seven and having them brought back by a constable half an hour later.—A second hand clothes dealer in Mersey-st., Mrs. Gibbon, said the prisoner pledged the boots at her shop, saying he had bought them.—P.C. Corcoran de- posed to apprehending the prisoner, who said he had bought the boots.—lie adhered to this statement, but was sent to jail for a month's hard labour.--Thomas Farley, of Daley's lodging-house, Scotland-road, was charged with stealing on Wednesday last a retriever dog the property of Peter Berry. Ship Canal labourer, who lives at the model lodging-house, Old Road.—The Chief Constable said the men were drinking together in the Vine Tavern on Tuesday night, and the prosecutor after- wards missed his dog. Next day he met the prisoner and asked him about the dog, and he said he knew nothing about the dog, but produced its collar from his pocket, and offered it to prosecutor, who refused to have it.—The Chief Constable reminded the Bench that there were innumerable thefts of dog collars in the town, and said this might be such a case.—The prosecu- tor said the dog had come back, and the prisoner had handed up the collar, therefore he did not wish to press the case.—The barman at the Vine Tavern said on Thursday morning the dog catne into the,vaults and lay down, and Farley was there and took the dog out, as he said, to find the owner.—The prisoner said he lost the dog.—D.S. Monaghan said the prisoner said he had picked up the collar, which he handed to him. He said he had offered it to the owner and he refused to have it. The Bench dealt with the prisoner only for stealing the collar, which had the owner's name on, and fined him 10s. and costs.
HAVING A GUN WITHOUT A. LICHNSH.—James Row- son, Back Stamford-st., was charged with using a gun without a license, near Orford Hall, on August 31st.,and was fined 20s. and costs.

DEFECTIVB PAsstisszs.—John Smith, Legh-st., was charged by Ralph Norman. inspector of nuisances, with having a dwelling-house, also a workshop in a defective condition. He was ordered to remedy their condition, and to pay costs. CHAROF.S AGAINST APPRENTICES.—Sarah Ellen Ellis and Elizabeth Lythgoe were summoned by John and Joseph Wilkinson, fustian cutters, on charges of absenting themselves from their work without leave. The cases were adjourned. NON-CONTRIBUTION Foe. Soris.—JohnCraddock, signal- man, and Peter Garland sen., Watkin-street, had orders made against them for non-contribution to their sons' maintenance, on the Clio and at St. Anne's Industrial School respectively.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
.... WHDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Z. Armitage (chairman), J. Tinslay, and Major Pickmere. RIDING WITHOUT RElNS.—Thomas Houghton for this offence on the 28th ult., at Croft, was fined 2. 6d. and costs.

KEEPING A Doa WITHOUT LICENSE.—Henry George Taylor, of Glazebrook, was charged with keeping a dog without license.—The defendant sent a letter claiming exemption as the dog was a sheep dog, but it appeared that he was not a farmer, though he lived at a farm. 10s. and costs.

CYCLING ON THE FOOTPATIL—Henry Manley, William Jackson, and Bertram Newcome were charged with rid- ing a bicycle on the footpath at Cuerdley, on the night of the 28th ult.—The defendants said there was no properly defined footpath. They were fined ss. each. POACHINO.—Edward Martin and William Allen. young men, were charged with trespassing on land in the occupation of John Bennett, at Burtonwood, on the 22nd ult.—Mr. White prosecuted on behalf of Mr. Fox Powys, owner of the land. A gamekeeper deposed to seeing the defendants with guns, shooting twice in the field.—The Chairman said the magistrates had not consider the case of poaching proved, but they had been trespassing and were fined 2s. 6d. and costs. -

div.head: SUICIDE OF AN UNDERURA.DUATE.
div.p: SUICIDE OF AN UNDERURA.DUATE.

On Thursday morning an undergraduate named Bryce was found dead in his room at Christ Church, Oxford, shot through the heart. A double-barrelled sporting gun was lying beside him, and a strap was fastened round the trigger and attached to the fender, pointing clearly to suicide. Mr. Bryce went up for examination on Wednesday, and was plucked in his viva voce trials. His parents reside at Bystock, near Exmouth.
REDUCTION IN WAGES IN IRELAND.

Notices have been served on all the employes in the engineering and shipbuilding concerns in Belfast of a general reduction of 10 per cent, on piecework, and from Is. to 2s. per week on fixed wages. The reduction by which 12,000 hands are affected, is to take effect one uonth from Saturday.

RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. KENDAL HORNETS.

The leading Westmoreland club are always favourites with visitors to Wilderspool, and it was not surprising, considering the unfavourable day on Saturday, to find that a large number had assembled to witness the first of the annual fixtures. Matches have been arranged now for the past five seasons, and on one occasion only can Kendal claim a decisive victory, this being the occa- sion of their making their debut on the Warrington ground. At that time they were indeed a clever com- bination, comprising such players as " Buff " Berry, Cross, Armstrong, and Walker. Still, despite the fact that importations of a wholesale character nave been made from the team, they still find players who are capable of holding their own in the best of company. The Hornets turned up at Warrington with an excellent team, and the homesters having Berry and Evans away, a capital game was anticipated.

It was 4.30 before Kendal kicked off towards the pavilion goal, Jolley heading the Warringtonians direct to the Hornets' quarters, Cassidy early on being com- pelled to concede a minor. The drop out afforded little relief, for Heesom, piloting the oval back, saw Hall res- pond for Webster to improve the homester's position. Mulling by the home backs gave Kendal a chance, and the half-way flag was reached, but the stay here was only of short duration, Nevins and Heesom, with judi- cious kicking, again reaching the Kendal line. From some smart passing by. Beard and Hill, Hall effected a. hi fine run through the tck of his opponents, but passing across to Railton, this player was soon grassed. A penalty kick to Warrington was of little advantage, and Whiteley punting to Boscow, the latter mulled the , greasy oval, Heesom saving in daring style five yards from the posts. Turner headed the forwards back to neutral ground, and a sequence of passes between Bate, Nevins and Webster saw Warrington once more on the aggressive. Hall again proved the saviour of his side, for a neat pass from Beard saw the Kendal centre oblige with a characteristic run, and neutral ground was again reached. A fine bout of exchange kicking was next I witnessed, Plumptoa, Heesom, and Renton being the leaders, the last-named finally finding touch at the War- rington quarter flag. Boseow made his mark in close quarters, and although he kicked well it had no effect on the determined attack now set up by the Kendal men, E. Wilson having a narrow shave for a score. Holmes was applauded for a gallant attempt to relieve, and Turner made his mark in response to Whiteley's kick. It was left to Bate to effect a substantial relief, and a fine run and pass to Plump- ton was taken finely by the latter, but he was forced into touch at the quarter flag. Railton and Frank Turner were next to the fore with short dribbles for their respective sides, whilst seine amusement was hereabouts caused by the antics of the players to main- tain hold of the ball. Ashton headed a rush, which looked long odds en scoring, Cassidy saving well. Plumpton next had a shot at goal from a mark, and a second minor being conceded, half time was called with the score—Warrington, 0-0-2 ; Kendal, nil. Frank Turner restarted, and soon Warrington exerted themselves, Donohue Jolley, and Thornley, beiug prominent in one rust, whicla culminated in a minor. Webster was to the fore with a mark, but Cassidy improved his side's portion by finding touch at centre. The home backs were next at fault, and as a consequence their quarters were reached ; but Heesom made up for the deficiency with a stylish run and kick, which reached the Hornets' quarters once more. At this point a sad accident befel Frank Turner, who fell with an opponent in touch, and the Warringtonian being underneath, had the misfortune te break his collar bone. The injured player was quickly conveyed to Liverpool, where the limb was set. Some brilliant exchanges were next witnessed, and Webster being the final recipient, he punted across the open, and putting his men quickly on one side, Jolley romped over the line for a clinking try, which point was further enhanced by Fair Turner from a difficult position. The restart saw the game being evenly contested, but the score would assuredly have been augmented had Webster received a pass in any- thing like decent form. A well executed dribble by Ashton was negatived by the off-side play of several of the forwards, but the kick did not avail the Hornets any for they were likewise a trifle too eager, and scrimmag- ing took place at the Kendal 25 flag. Plumpton now made a bold bid for a score, a minor accruing from the effort. Donohue and Jolley were to the fore in some loose play, Cassidy staving off the effort by an accurate kick. Again Plumpton was applauded for .a fine run, and the same player had a shot at goal a few minutes from the call of time, and no addition to the score being forthcoming, an enjoyable game ended as—Warrington, 1-0-3 ; Kendal Hornets, nil. Teams :—Warrington : Boscow, back ; Plumpton, Heesom, and Webster, three-quarter backs ; John Rate, and Nevins, half-backs ; H. Ashton, Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, J. Jolley, Donohue, Holmes, Tears, Thornley, and Bandies, forwards. Kendal Hornets: Cassidy, 'back ; Railton, Hall, and Whiteley, three-quarter backs ; Beard and Hill. half-backs: Harrison, Nicholson, Simm, ; W. Wilson, R. Wilson, C. Wilson, Dickenson, Fisher, and E. Hine, forwards. WARRINGTON A. v. Faitswoirru OLD SM.—Notwith- standing the threatening state of the elements the visit of the Warringtonians attracted a large number of enthusiasts to the Failsworth ground, which was found to be in a very bad condition. The commencement was an eye-opener, for after the visitcrs had started the con- test, the ball was returned, Mad a long loose dribble carried the ball over the line, Mariana getting a try. Although Warrington forced the game to mid-field, the Old Boys, stimulated by their early success and the shouts of their supporters, returned to the attack. Ashurst cleared splendidly, and Barnes, throwing out te Daniels a judicious piece of work, enabled Warrington to gain a foothold well inside the home half. The warfare was of the liveliest possible character at this point, several quick displays of passing by Warrington, in which Smith, Lally, Barnes, and Westall were notable, calling forth applause. Again the Old Boys by strong rushes threatened disaster, but the visiting forwards stuck determinedly to their work, and eventually Lally, Beckley, and Hampson relieved. Still the play ram- paged abOut the visitors' half, but Ashurst was in grand form, clearing his lines beautifully. Then Glover, Bradbury,Edwards,and Molyneaux were instrumental in pressing back the dashing bomesters, only to see Chad- wick and his fellow three-quarters by some long kick- ing change the venue to the opposite end of the ground. Warrington had all their work cut out to keep Failsworth at bay, until a kick by Daniels found touch at centre, and half-time was called with Failsworth 0-1-1 to nil. Directly after the resumption of hostilities, Smith and Lally got the ball away beautifully to Barnes, who effected a grand run right to the line and a minor was shortly conceded, whilst after some heavy scrimmaging another was given. A vigorous rush by Davies, Forster, Buckley, and Higham, was responded to by Henthorn, with the result that the centre line was reached. Whilst the struggle was raging here, Lally secured the leather and, slipping round the scrimmage, passed to Smith, who smartly flung across to Barnes, and the latter with one of his old cup-tie efforts dodged two or three opponents and scudded away to the line, gaining a brilliant try, which he supplemented by placing a goal. Again through the efforts of Hampson, Bradbury, Molyneaux, and Davies the Old Boys had to defend, a capital screw kick by Lane, however, clearing. A dribble by the home forwards was saved in the nick of time by Ashurst, but Failsworth had gained a footing they had been longing for. A desperate struggle between both sets of forwards ensued, Warrington having an anxious few minutes. Ultimately Ashurst and Barnes I relieved the tension, and Glover, Edwards, Buckley; and Hampton rushed into Failsworth lines. A determined onslaught was made by the visitors, but when a try I seemed certain off-side spoiled the opportunity and a free kick enabled the defenders to stave off the impend- ing danger, the whistle blowing leaving Warrington victors of a hard match by 1-0-2 to 0-1-1. SALFORD v. RUNCORN.—PIayed at Salford, before 4,000 spectators. Both teams were fairly well represented. At 3.45 Kent kicked off for Salford, and Faulkner re- turned. After a good kick by Houghton, France and Fox ran well to the visitors' 25. A rush by the Runcorn forwards took play to the centre, where France and Walsh were to the front. Crompton, however, got in a nice kick, and the leather landed in touch in the home quarters. Crompton, the Runcorn centre, had now to retire hurt and Faulkner took his place. On setting to work again France got hurt and Crompton returned. Some grand play was next witnessed in midfield when Houghton relieved with a grand kick to Salford 25. After a few tight packs half time was called with the score nil. Faulkner restarted for Runcorn, and Man- waring returned. A lot of even play took place in mid- field, and then Barrett, following up his own kick, ran in behind the posts, Walsh improving. On resuming Kent and France put in a capital dribble, but Houghton neutralised. Faulkner now retired, which left Runcorn with only 14 men. Abrams was next prominent with a grand dribble to the "Reds'" quarters but Walsh kicked well down the field, and Houghton, having his kick charged let the homesters into the Runcorn 25. A rush by the visitors took play to centre. Crompton and J. Robinson next shone conspicuously, but Fox relieved. A free kick to Salford caused the Runcorn quarters to be invaded, but Crompton came to the rescue. Good play by Craven, Barrett, and Miles resulted in the latter scor- ing. Walsh failed to improve. On resumino. Runcorn attacked, but Miles defended well and from a'long kick by Houghton a minor resulted for Runcorn.

Runcorn ::Houghton, back; Pendlebury, Crompton, and T. Robinson, three-quarter backs; G. Robinson and Abrams, half backs; Williams, Riley, Faulkner, Hamp- son, Davies, Moores, Langley, A. and S. Taylor, for- wards.

Salford: Manwaring, back; Fox, Barrett, and Miles, three-quarter backs; Walsh and France, half backs; Kent, King, Roberts, Casey, Brierley, Cartwright, A. Knowles, F. Knowles, and J. Craven, forwards.

WIDNES Y. MILLOII.—The above teams faced each other on Saturday, on the Lowerhouse-lane ground. The elements were somewhat threatening, and conse- quently affected the attendance. Brennan started the leather, a scrimmage ensuing immediately. Forster then picked up, and gave a neat pass to Barber, who made the most of it, placing the oval safely home, before the game had been in progress two minutes. Farmer took the kick, and easily improved the point. It was pleas- ing to witness a fine passing game, which soon rushed the oval into the opponents' quarters again; but the visitors returned. When in mid-field Wright made a smart ru,., but the defence was too strong. The visitors played up well, and a brave attempt was made to score. A short time afterwards, however, Wilkinson placed over the line, but the attempt at goal was unsuccessful. Both teams played vigorously, and when near the line one of the visitors picked up and ran over, but to all appear- ances the ball was knocked on. The referee allowed the point, but the endeavour to improve was fruitless. This spurred the homesters on, and some smart play was witnessed, when Alford, the new acqui- sition to the Widnes organization, made a splendid run from almost midfield, and scored. Farmer failed to improve this time. When the whistle sounded half-time, the score was—Widnes, one goal, one try ; Millom, two tries. The game continued of a very even natnre, and was centred in midfield, nothing worthy of note occurring, with the exception of two or three smart attempts to gain ground, with the result that the leather was kicked ia touch-in-goal by the Widneaians. Alford made his mark, but nothing came of it. The oval was then rushed down the field by the homesters, and a determined effort was made to score, but the ball was kicked dead. Time was then called, the home team being victorious by one goal, one try (seven points), to two tries (four points). Teams : Widnes : Full back, Hartles ; three-quarter backs, Alford, Drummond, and Brennan ; half backs, Barber and Wright ; forwards, Hewitt, Gordon, Whelan, John- son, Emery, H. Farmer, Hogan, Forster, and VVynnes. Millom : Full back, Bell ; three-quarter backs, Hodgson Buckett, and Wilkinson ; half backs, Armstrong and Guine ; forwards, Whelan, Burns, Warburton, Fawcett, Bosse, Williams, Adderson, Robinson, and J. Fawcett.

RUNCORN v. SALFORD "A " MAlM—Played at Run- corn, on Saturday, in a heavy downpour of rain. Antrobus kicked off, and quick following up by the homesters prevented a return. Salford quickly asserted themselves, and Dunvaband was lucky in saving. Even play followed, until a bad miss by Houghton gave the visitors an opening, Limb being forced to kick dead. Following the drop out, Lightfoot ran strongly, until pushed into touch by Barrett. Scrimmaging followed, until Ditchfield got possession, and some pretty passing between the visitors, ended in Campbell getting a good try. W. Oswald took the place, and succeeded in kick- ing a goal. The re-start saw Dunvaband to the fore with a good dribble, and the Salford quarters were invaded, but Oswald was safe, and with a good kick removed the danger. Lightfoot dribbled well, but little headway could be made until a passing movement between Faulkner, Antrobus, and Limb removed play to centre. C. Oswald passed out to Bowker, but Antrobus cleverely intercepted, and play was taken to the Salford line. Exciting play now followed for some minutes, until a strong rush by the visiting forwards cleared the danger. Haf-time arrived with the score— Salford. one goal ; Runcorn, nil. Campbell re-started, to which Dunvaband replied. Webbe made an effort to get through, but was safely held, and tall kicking between the respective backs, ended in the ball going into touch near the home quarter flag. From a line out, Derbyshire got well away, but Oswald effected a clever save. Bowker ran strongly, but passing between Dunvaband, Faulkner, and Antrobus again threatened the Salford lined. The home forwards now played up strongly, and Warder getting possession, dropped a pretty goal. Even play followed this for some time, until a misunderstanding between Houghton and Limb, enabled Salford to score an easy try, from which W. Oswald again placed with success. The game ended in a win for Salford, by 2-0-0 to 1-0-0. Teams:— Runcorn : Houghton, full back ; A. Limb, Warder and A. N. Other, threequarter backs; Dunvaband and Faulkner, half-backs ; Antrobus, Derbyshire, Webbe, Clucas, Evans, Gayter, Lawson. Jordan, and Lightfoot, forwards. Salford : W. Oswald, full back ; Barrett, Bowker, and Lightfoot, threequarter hacks; C. Oswald and Ditchfield, half-backs ; Haslatn, Tonge, Horrocks, Hindehaw, Tattersall, Campbell, Cooke, Wilson, and R. Oswald, forwards. WIGAN RIICRRATION •. WARRINGTON RANGHRS.— , Played at Wigan on Saturday in wretched weather. The home team lost the toss, and Green commenced opera- tions by across kick, but the Rangers broke through, and Walkden saving well stopped the rush. The visitors continued to press for some time, and eventually forced a minor. The Recs. now played up, and good work by Walkden and Forster took the game to the other end, but Hamblett relieved finely, and again the Rangers at. tacked s:rongly, and from a scrimmage smart passing by Savage, Clark, and Warburton allowed the latter to score a clever try, which Clark converted into a goal. After the interval forward play became the main fea- ture of the game, and in this department the Rangers fairly excelled themselves. Their quick following up and sure tackling upset the calculations of the home team, who,encouraged by the shouts of their supporters, made great efforts to equalize, but the splendid kicking and defensive play of the visitors' back nullified any good intention the homeaters had, and for the first time this season the Recs. succumbed to the superiority of their opponents, the Rangers finally winning an excit- ing game by one goal one minor to nil.

WARRINGTON RANGIIRS 2ND V. LOGSDALV ROVIIRS IST. —This match was played on the Lovely-lane enclosure en Saturday, rain falling heavily. The homesters held the upper hand throughout. Caldwell scoring a try and McCue landing a goal from the place, the game finally resulting in a victory for the Rangers by one goal three minors to Lugsdale nil.

DALLAM BREWERY (V.) WARRINGTON Sr. MARY'S 2111 D TEAMS.—This match was played on Brewery ground on Saturday in very heavy rain. The Visitors scored an easy try, and placed s goal.—Final Scorn: St. Mary's 1 goal, 3 minors to nil. WARRINGTON Sr. MARY'S (V.) DALLAM BREWERY FIRST TRAMS.—This match should have been played on Saturday last, but owing to the heavy rain the match was postponed.
TIIM 0' PEG'S WELCOME TO PEEL GREEN. Cowl Nyowton friends, no deaubt yore wond'rin' Heaw aw'm getten' on i'th' new shop ; An' whether aw'm deawn i' my meawth, or
Beginnin' to like it " first chop." ' Well, aw've bin i' sum hunderts o' places,

An' mony fresh faces aw've seen; But aw think, lads, i' aw my experience There's nowt, up to neaw, byets Peel Green. To say that they're deawnreet warm hearted, Is only to gie um ther due; An' aw fund eawt thay dunnot hawf relish lo see a new friend lookin' " blue." An' one i' partickler aw'st mention, Amung aw the lot that aw've seen, Wo wuz kindness its& to my kindred An' me, wen we 000 m to Peel Green. But my friend, aw've no deaubt, witin't like it, To tigger too plain i' my verse; Tho' he's known aw reawnd here to be ready Wi' oather his honds or his purse. Fro' Lunnon to Nyowton God bless o', An' aw the known places between, Tole noan find a finer example Than my earliest friend i' Peel Green. On the Bowin' Green close to my digging, Aw wcz welcomed va cheers an' smiles • An' i' th' gam's that aw played single-honded, Aw wuz not run away wi fer Miles But wen th' dubbles coom on, eawr owd Cheerm on, An' Turn—yore owd Turn—cud be seen Doin' justice to Bashaw's good teychin', At " shootin' " and play at Peel Green. But eawr doom, it wur rayther soon seaunded, An' wen welly th' last chances hed gone, Eawr Captain strowlt o'er to a player,

An' reniarkt, " Nathan, theau'arth.e moo! Theau's bin playin' wi' tb. bull till he's getten His burns wheer thay shudn't be seen; An' neaw, dost see, Victory's restin' Wi' th' yung'st Captain's team at Peel Green."

_ At neet, ther wuz grand aungs an' speeches— An' proposin's by " Tommy," wee! said; Followed up by eaur Vicar's discoorsin' On the subject o' " Life's tickle thread." Well, that's aw, lads, an' aw'm wee! contented
W;' aw that aw've heerd an' seen; An " aw hope to be theer on Setterdays," Wen Convivials are on i' Peel Green. TIM 0' PEGS.
