div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

The "Athletic News" says: Warrington are receiving a lot of very unfair criticism at present, and following the Swinton match a report was circulated that they played a rough game against Stockport on Monday. In connection with this match Mr. Warren, the secretary, wrote the referee asking his opinion, and has received a reply that he saw nothing out of the way in the play of tho Warrington men.

Football has its fascinating powers, adds the same paper, and like most pleasures and pursuits, it is the element of danger that enhances the delight, but we question whether some of the Warrington players feel many thrills of happiness. No fewer than three of the members of that well-known organisation are suffering from broken collar bones. "Smack" Bate was the first to slide on the injured list ; he was followed by Lawless on Saturday week, and now Frank Turner is placect among the injured. There must have been some collar- ing done, and yet time are people going about asserting that Warrington play a rough game.

The League was again in full swing on Saturday afternoon. The attendances were so satisfactory in each case except at West Bromwich that we append the figures : Everton v. Aston Villa 15.000 Sheffield Wednesday. v. Burnley 12,000 Sunderland v. Stoke Bolton Wan. v. Wolverhampton Wan. 7,000 Derby County v. Notts Forest 9,000 Notts County •. Preston North End lO,OOO Blackburn Rovers v. Accrington 7,000 West Bromwich Albion v. Newton Heath 3,000 69,000

div.head: We have thus a grand total of 69,000, which is-Clo—q-uent testimony to the popularity of the League.
div.p: We have thus a grand total of 69,000, which is-Clo—q-uent testimony to the popularity of the League.

To Notts Forest belongs the credit of the only victory obtained away from home. ' f was, moreover, their first League victory at home or abroad, so that they have good reason to congratulate themselves. They did not win because they caught Derby County with a weak team, as the two Goodalls were in their i!olace. Which- ever way the result is looked at It is full of satisfaction from a " reds' " point of view, and we may expect them to enter into future engagements with plenty of confi- dence.

Russell shaped so well with his new comrades against Blackpool on Thursday, that the North End team were expected to do great things at Trent Bridge,on Saturday, more especially as Gordon was back in his place. But once again things did not come out as calculated, and history repeated itself, insomuch as Notts won the encounter by two goals, as they did twelve months ago. In this tespect the Prestonians are no worse off as com- pared with last season. They will not have a chance of revenge until the 31st of March.

Sunderland already occupy the best position in the League, this coming about owing to the failure of the North end at Nottingham. The champions have omy missed one point in five engagements, as against their Preston rivals a couple in six fixtures. Sunderland had Stoke for visitors on Saturday, and Sent them home beaten by two goals, just as they did in the same match at the Wearside last season. The Potters invariably give their big opposents a good game, and that of Sat- urday was no exception to the general rule. The Stoke defence was seen at its very best, and that means a good deal, as most clubs know.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The. fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. J. Mclntyre presided, and there were present Messrs. J. Stokes, J. Bagu- lev, E. Aaron, T. Lewis,H. E. Heywood, J. Whittam, J. Knowles, E. Bretherton, J. Smith, J. M. Williams J. Parr, James Brandreth, T. Baxter. J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (assistant clerk), J. Farrington, (nuisance inspector), and Dr. Adams (medical officer). THR NIIISANCH INSPECTOR.

The Local Government Board formally sanctioned the appointment of Mr. James Farrington as inspector of nuisances for the district for the ensuing year, at a salary of £l4O per annum. TYPHOID FEVER IN THE DISTRICT. The Local Government Board wrote stating that they were informed by the Registrar General that between July 7th and September 23rd, 11 deaths from typhoid fever were registered in the registration sub-district of Runcorn, part of which was comprised within the Run- corn Rural Sanitary district. They requested that the Sanitary Authority would instruct their medical officer of health, to prepare a report upon the recent prevalence of fever in their district. The report should contain such information as could be given with regard to the number of non-fatal as well as the fatal cases, and to the circumstances in which they had occurred, with reference particularly to the purity of the water used for drinking, to the drainage, and to the method of disposal of excrement in the localities where the disease has been prevalent. It should also state the measures taken by the Sanitary Authority, or the Medical Officer of Health, for checking the spread of the disease. The Board did not find that the outbreak had been reported by the doctor. The Medical Officer said he was preparing a report on the matter for the information of the Board. It was not an outbreak ; there were a number of cases isolated from each other, and all these cases had been reported to the Board.—The Clerk said he would reply to the communication tos that effect.

CHOLERA REGULATIONS. The Local Government Board writing with regard to cholera regulations as to vessels bound for Runcorn, stated that as a result of the conference with the Port Sanitary Authority of Liverpool it was understood that in the case of infected vessels bound for the docks within the jurisdiction of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority the officers at Liverpool would move them and deal with them. NAUSEATING NUISANCE AT FRODSHAM. A letter was read from Mr. T. A. Rigby describing the offensive and nauseous smell.arising from the man- holes of the main sewer at 0 7erton, and asking that steps should be taken to remedy the nuisance. Mr. Heywood and Mr. Williams corroborated Mr. Rigby's statement.—The matter was referred to the Frodshare Parochial Committee.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. Monks (chairman), and Aldermen Francomb, Sutton, and Wright, John Craddock, licensed victualler, Vine Tavern, Market Place., was charged with having, on the 23rd ult., allowed certain intoxicating liquors to be consumed on his premises, during the time when such pre- mises should have been closed in conformity with the licensing Act of 1874. namely between 12 p.m. and 1.30 a.m. John Marsh, licensed victualler, Lord Rodney Inn, Winwick-street, George Lunt, of the Theatre Tavern, Scotland-road, Thomas Peak, of the Golden Grove Inn, and Joseph Craik, clerk, 37, Arpley-street, were charged with being unlaw- fully cm Craddock's premises at the time. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defendants, all of whom except Craik were employed by Messrs. Walker and Sons, brewers, and Mr. J. Longland watched the case on behalf of the Warrington Temperance Federation.— Police Sergeant Smith said about 12.30 on the morning of September 23rd, he was in Lime-street, and heard the sound of voices in the Vine Tavern. He listened, and heard footsteps in the bar, and jingling of glasses. About a quarter te one, and again at five minutes past one, he saw Win. Pritchard, manager for Craddock, pas- sing glasses from the bar to the bar parlour. He heard talk going on continually. He heard footsteps coming up Golden Grove-street, and concealed himself by one of the fish market pillars, and saw two ladies come up, and knock at the side door of the inn, and the manager Win. Pritchard, open it. He was in company with Marsh. Witness walked into the bar parlour, and sitting there past a partition saw Lunt, Craik, and Peak. There were glasses there containing liquor. Craik had his in his hand. Be said "Hullo, sergeant, come and and have a cigar." He replied " Not on this occasion," and asked him what he was doing there. He then asked Mr. Pritchard what he was doing with those men there at that time of the morning. He said "We are all friends ; we have been to Manchester, and we came up together. Of course he is an old friend of ours. I did not like to deny him and he followed us in, and of course I did not like to tell him to go home. " Don't say nowt about it." He said" what are you going to have to drink ? " Witness replied that he did not drink, and said "Don't tempt me to have anything." You will only make your case worse. " Get these men out ot these premises." He then walked out, and Pritchard followed him out and asked him to take no further notice of the matter. Ho went in to put Craik out, and in five minutes came out again and said," Well sergeant what are you going to do 1'" He added" Do look over it." Witness replied " I thought you had gone to get that man out." He went in to do this, and came out again, Lunt following him. Lunt pleaded with witness for Pritchard, saying he had a wife and five children, bilk it did not matter for himself, as he was a single man. Pritchard cleared the house and it then being about half-past one, began pleading with witness again. He said the first round was not paid for, although it should have been, and the second round Lunt promised to pay for at the month's end. He saw through the F keyhole, before he entered the house, five glasses on the table. He could not see how many there were on the tray.—By Mr. Browne : There is an inner door which must have been open, for me to see what I did.—Mr. Browne : It has a Chubb's lock which can't be seen through.—Witness, further cross-examined : He did not hear any work going on in the cellar. He did not see Marsh and Peak go in. The ladies who knocked at the door were their wives, he understood. Marsh was on the doorstep when they came.—ln reply to the chairman, Mr. Browne said the owner had for private reascns ceased to live at the Vine Tavern for the present, but would live there again.—William Pritchard said on the night in question he returned from Manchester with Craik, by the train due at Warrington at 11.37. They walked up the street together and when they got to the Vine Tavern, he asked Craik to come in and wait a few minutes as he had some cellar work to do for the morning, and they could walk home together afAer, as they lived in the same road. He came inside and sat in darkness, and witness went into the cellar eo ae, his work. He heard a knock at the dem' and ansWered it and found Lunt there, who said What are ynat doing here, Pritchard. now?" Witness asked them in, and Lunt said "Let's have a light on the subject," and lit the gas. Witness went into the cellar again, and soon after answered an- other knock at the door and found Marsh and Peak there, who said they had come out to fetch their wives, who were visiting. They went in, and when witness had finished his cellar work, said "Well, while we are here you,might as well have a drink.", They each had a small gin,.except Laird, who had la ,bottie of.l3ass's beer, and afterwards he said" We will just haveanOther and then go," and they had the same again. Illeyfia talk- ing and smoking, and then another knock carnb' at the door, and he found Mrs. Marsh and MM. Peak there. Sergeant Smith walked across, and said to him "What are you doing here now ? " Witnefaltold him he was at liberty to look through the house.:At;n request of the sergeant he got all his visitors out.-.lht „eller Chief Con- stable : He should have accountbd Tor the drinks.—By Mr: Browne : He supplied none till Mail* And Peak came in. Lunt was in the habit of calling for him that they I might go home together. There was a Chubb's lock on ' the inner door, and it WAS always kept closed. There was a spring lock on it that would prevent it being kept open.—By the Chief Constable: He had said he was not aware he was doing anything wrong in having the men on the premises. It was contrary to his employers' in- structions.—The Chief Constable: flow was it you asked the policeman to say nothing about it P—Alderman Sutton: He thought he had got into a difficulty, and he wanted to get oat of it.—Mr. Browne then addressed the Bench. He said the defendants had been summoned under a part of a sub-section under which by itself no summons had, to his knowledge, ever before been taken out. The summons was invari- ably taken out for selling drink, or exposing for sale, or keeping open, or permitting drinking during prohibited hours," and then the words" or allowing intoxicating liquors to be consumed during prohibited hours" were brought in only for the purpose of supplying any missing link. The prosecution could not prove there was keep- ing open to sell drink, and admitted there was no selling, therefore there was no case to answer. He admitted that the police had a perfect right to bring the case, but by the Amendment Act of 1874, Pritchard was perfectly justified in providing liquor for his own friends, at his own expense. Mr. Craddock was not responsible, moreover, for the acts of his servant in allowing drink to be consumed on his premises during probibited hours, and there had not been a single case upholding the con- trary view. Mr. Browne quoted an opinion of Stone, a legal authority, that an employer was not criminally responsible for the act of his servant, unless he did some illegal act, out of which his master made a profit.— George Lunt corroborated Pritchard's statement, that no drink was paid for.—The Bench, after about ten minutes' retirement. fined Craddock 20s. and costs, recommending that someone should live on his premises, and dismissed the other defendants.—Mr. Browne gave notice of appeal against Craddock's convi, n.

. „ ASYLUM CHARGES. Mr. Arthur C. Procter, Clerk to the Committee of the Parkside Asyluin, Macclesfield, wrote enclosing the following resolution, passed at the meeting of the committee of visitors of the Asylum, held on the 22ad July last.—" That as from the first day of October next, the weekly charge to the Cheshire Unions be increased from Bs. sfrd., to 9s. 4d." With reference thereto, Mr. Proctor pointed out. (Ist) That having regard to the' decision of Mr. Justice North, in the recent actton of Proctor, v. the Cheshire County Council and otherS, the Committee were not at liberty to apply any rotion of the fund with reference to which such action svaB brought—reducing the future weekly charge to the Unions below the actual weekly cost of their patients. (2nd) That it appeared from the printed ace"nts the year ending 31st March last, that the avera*, weekly cost per patient during such year, was Bs. llid. (3rd) That the effect of the recent decision of the Queen:e Bench Division, in the case of " Queen V. Dolby,"S that the rates on the asylum will, in future, be charge- able against the unions, instead of the county. rho rates last year, on Parkside Asylum, amounted to about £5OO, which sum was last year paid by the county. Mr. Brandreth said the charge at the Upton Asylurn,_ was 7g., and he thought it was unfair that they should have to send to Parkside, at a higher figure, simply because the institution at Upton was occupied by patients from the city of Chester.

TER IMMIGRATION OF PAUPER ALIENS. Mr. J. Owen Perry, clerk to the Hackney Union, forwarded a copy of a letter, the Guardians had for- warded to the president of the Local Government Board, upon the unrestricted immigration of destitute aliens, and asked if the Guardians of Runcorn Union agreed with the object to petition in a similai manner. The letter mentioned drew attention to the grave dangers that threaten the health and well-being of the commun- ity, through the unrestricted immigration of destitute alien,and urged that the Local Government Board should obtain pswers from Parliament to prevent its continu- ance. Instances in suOport of this contention were :Oven* and the letter concluded—" Without multiplying evid- ence this Board would respectfully suggest that the time for action, contemplated by the Common* Committee, has arrived, as on all sides, testimony abounds of the supplanting of native labour by cheap foreign and of the unfortunate competition by foreigners mak- ing the struggle for existence so keen that too often the - native toiler breaks down mentally and p`ivsically under laWur, the undue strain, and retires beaten from the unequal strife to spsnd the remainder of life in the seclusion of an asylum, a state of things becoming more general and so painfully attested by the fearful increase of lunacy among the struggling poor and trading classes."—The Chairman said this was a very large and very itnPort- ant question.—Mr. Williams said lie was present at the Poor Law Conference at Chester, when this question was fully discussed. A resolution was come to slightly different to the one suggested by the Hackney Union, to the effect that the Government should be requested to so far interfere with the immigrat ion of destitute alien.% as to prevent people landing on our shores who had ne ostensible means of subsistence, or any friends to go b°, and who were likly to be a charge on the poor r ALM That foreigners did carry into our large towns a vast amount of filth and abominations, no person who had lived for many years in Manchester could deny. They reduced the physical, moral, and social qualities of the population. Foreigners also broke down the prices in the labour market He gave notice that at the next meeting he would bring forward a resolution on the subject, not exactly on the lines laid down by the , Hackney Union. Thus has passed away, in his seventy-eighth year, one of the foremost Frenchmen of letters of the centurit who in the domain of history and religious philosophy occupied as unique a position as that enjoyed by the late Victor Hugo in the province of poetry and imagina" tive prose.

CDtrEL ARAB SLAVE HipmElm—The Arab System of raiding is unique. About 50 years ago they subdued the extensive Manyema country, of which Nyangwe and Kassongu are now well-known centres. The Manyemas, after being thus • disbanded, gradually allied themselves with the Arabs, and eventually have spread their operations • throughout the country to an enormous extent. ' The Arabs, on their expeditions in search of slaves and ivory, generally surround the native villages early in the morning. At a given signal they rush in from all points, firing right and left, and capturing all the women. If the men offer resistance they are shot, otherwise they are allowed to escape. The marauders then pillage all the huts in the village, which they afterwards fire. If, how- ever, the place happens to be extensive, the Arabs adopt different tactics. They form a stockade or zareba. Thus fortified they establish themselves, maintaining a strict watch at night. During the whole of their stay they keep this attitude of defence. After the lapse of several days they release two or three of the women prisoners, who are instructed to deliver a message to the men—in hiding far away in the forest—to the effect that if they want their women back they must come and redeem them with tusks of ivory—each woman being valued at the rate of one large tusk. Then several days pass, until perhaps one morning early a gruff voice is heard in the distance hailing the encampment. He inquires as to the truth of the statement brought by the women, and then follows a parley. During the subsequent days the persecuted natives come with Ivory to redeem their mothers, sisters, or wives. Eventaally they make friends with their conquerors, vim° then use them as guides to the next encamp- ment, where the same treatment is repeated upon , the neighbours of those recently plundered. Part of the reward that the guides receive from the Arabs s. is the flesh of the people who are shot in the next attack.—From "Life Among Congo Savages," by Herbert Ward, in Scribner.

THE SEAL AND His JACKET.—As received, the skin is not in the least like what it will be. The fur that is prized so much is to the seal what the down is to the bird, and it is hidden entirely by a coat of stiff over-hair—dull, grey, and grizzled. The salt is first washed off; the fat is then removed, the eking are then washed, and the grease and water removed by the knife; and then they are tacked on frames to keep them smooth, and dried in a mod er.te heat. They are then soaked in water and thoroughly cleansed with soap, and then, after another drying, the warm skin is placed over a beam, and the hair removed with a knife. When all the hair is out, the skins are dried, then damped, and then shaved. They are then stretched, Worked and dried, and softened in a fulling mill, or trodden with bare feet in a barrel, the workmen dancing upon them to break them into leather, While the grease is absorbed with hard wood saw- dust that from time to time he dusts in. The skins are then dyed, the dye being put on with a brush. They are then dried and dyed again, and dried again and dyed again, until they are of the desired Colour, sometimes eight or twelve coats of dye , being required. They are then shaved down to the proper thickness, softened again in a hogshead, and sometimes run in a revolving cylinder, with fine sawdust to clean them. With all these many Processes and freightages, no wonder that the finished fur costs as many pounds as it brought Pence to the killers on the Pribylovs. Leisure Hour.

ARISTOCRACY AND TRADE IN THE OLD DAYS.— ..if& family may be ruined by extravagance, but it is tot always through rain that the representatives of a family are to be found in humble, or compara- tively humble circumstances; but that the junior members of a gentle family went into trade. The occasion of that eruption of false pride relative to "soiling the hands with trade," was the great Change that ensued after Queen Anne's reign. When the trade of the country grew, great fortunes Were made in business, at the same time that the landed gentry had become impoverished, first through their losses in the Civil War, then by the extravagance of the period of the Restoration, together with drinking and gambling. Vast num- bers of estates changed hands, passed away from the old aristocracy into the possession of men who had amassed fortunes in trade, and it was among the children of these rich, retired tradesmen that there sprang up such a contempt for whatever savoured of the shop and the counting house.—" Old Country Li/e," by S. Baring Gould. , TRUE WOMANLY CULTURE.—There is no more •',,. lovely or beautiful sight on earth than a well . educated and truly cultivated young girl or woman. She can almca,.- alwa.,s be recognised, the first glance. It is not necessary that she be beautiful to be attractive even to the casual observer. True culture, culture that includes the heart as well as the intellect, that elevates and gives self poise and dignity to the whole nature, always leaves its tlnpress upon face and manner. Repose is one of its essential characteristics; unobtrusiveness is tuiother. During his later year, old Dr. Walter Charming, of Boston, was fond of finding me at leisure, and gaining possession of my great old office-chair for a chat And chats they were to be remembered The world will grow to be very much older than it is now before it bears upon its bosom a physician more honest and sincere in his practice, or more.. devoted to his patients. Aniong the numerous professional anecdotes related to me by the doctor (and I have given many of them ere this) was the following, and he said it was literally true as he told it, the patient was as honest in his planning as honest could be: Old Johnny Grey, we call him, after a long life devoted to the buying and selling of odds and ends of every description—old junk : old furniture; and old everything—had amassed quite a fortune, and concluded to settle down and enjoy it, to give up businecs and live like a gentleman. Well, he sold oil', and shut up shop, and began the life of ease and comfort, and he got along very well. He never was a miser, never was a niggard, though he was not a man of broad benevolence; but he did a great many generous things in a small, quiet way, and lived very comfortably. But, after a time, as hi years increased, and as the adipose tissue became superabundant, he began to ail, and he called upon Dr. Clianning to give him help. The good doctor paid him a visit, and gave to his case careful study mad critical judgment. Proper medicines were prescribEd, and, beyond this, there must be physical exercise. The man was growing dangerously fat, and the muscles were becoming limp and flaccid. Said the doctor, after the medicine lied been provided for: "Mr. Grey, you must take exercise. In your case it is an absolute necessity. Now let me lay it down for you: Here you are, right in sight of the Common (Boston Common). On every pleasant day—every day when the weather will let you go out—do you walk arouni the Common. It will do you more good than all the medicine in the world. My medicine will help you, but that will help you more. Will you do it ? " Johnny said he would give it a trial. It looked dubious to him, but be would do it, if he could. And so the doctor left him. The following day chanced to be clear and bright, and as Charming happened to be riding past the old fellow's dwell- ing just at nightfall, he thought he woula look in, and see how the walk had succeeded. He found Mr. Grey propped up in his great easy chair, with a bowl of hot punch at his elbow. "Well, Mr. Grey, did you try the walk to- day?" "Yes, doctor," replied the old man, with a deeply-drawn breath; "I tried it, but I couldn't quite make it work. I get just hcdf way round, when I found it was coming hard on me, and I had to turn, and comeback I" 8.0.

div.head: TRUE MANHOOD
div.p: TRUE MANHOOD

-- - It is a simple story, but its lesson of live is I worth treasuring up. I blame no man for being proud of noble ancestors. The man who is proud of his father's honours may be justly proud- but when he fancies that ancestry can cover faults succeeding generations, he makes a mistake. He who is a pensioner upon the reputation of the dead. has but a poor inheritance. "Honour and shame from no condition size; Act well your part, there all the honour lies."
