div.head: Retttrs to the Obitor.
div.p: Retttrs to the Obitor.
ST. MICHAELS CHURCH, RUNCORN.

Sir,—lt appears that Bishop Jayne consecrated this place last Thursday, although he knew previously that images of Christ, the Virgin Mary and the Apostle John had been set up, and Canon Wood was also aware o' the satne. I question very much whether some of the donors would have given a penny to the buileEng had they known such things would eventually be placed in the chancel. Bishop Jayne and Co., should read the thirty-nine articles. The thirty-fifth calls such thin,,s Malls, saying: " Woe be to the erector, setter-up, a d maintainer of images in churches and temples; for a greater penalty remaineth for him than the death of the body." So that images in churches and idolatry go always both together, and that therefore the one cannot be avoided, except the other, specially in all public plans, be destroyed. Wherefore, to make images, and publicly to set them up in the temples and churches, places appointed peculiarly to the service of God, is to make images to the use of religion." Churchmen, to know what the teaching of theChureh of England is, must study the articles. October 4, 1892.
WATCHMAN.

div.head: TILE POLICE PROSECUTION OF PUBLICANS
div.p: TILE POLICE PROSECUTION OF PUBLICANS
IN WARRINGTON.

Sir,—l am glad to notice that the police are on the alert to take notice of any infringement of the Licensing Acts on the part of publicans in this town. Evidence of this was furnished on Monday last in the Borough court. am also glad that for once the Bench made up their minds to convict. Usually they have found a reason for not doing so, and I find it rather diffix it to believe that if the houses and licenses in question had heel% ttreenall's instead of Walker's, the Bench would not once more have found a similar reason. lam sorry to say this; but the recent and most unmistakable evidence the town has had of the pat tiality of the Borough Bench for Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. over all other brewers puts these suspicions into the mind.- The Bench must bear the criticism, and the suspicion awakened by their own conduct. My egret at that affair is all the greater becanse three Libera . justices were patty to it. There was a day when Mr. Monks, J.P., would have acted very differently, but the air of Walton has had a relaxing effect ! I cannot otherwise account for the change. My objecz, however, in this letter is to ask whether, in such cases as these, brought forward by the police last Monday,the pr.)secution should not have bean in the hands of the Town Clerk, or of some solicitor instructed by him ? This appears to me to be a desirable course. It would immensely strengthen the hands of the police to know that they would be officially upheld by the Town Authorities. We need to see more vigour and determination imported into the management of this matter, and I hope that next time the Chief Constable has a case of this kind the Town Clerk will be there to prosezute it. —Yours faithfully,
JOHN YONGE.
13, Wilson Patten-st., October 4, 1892. JUSTICES' JUSTICE AT THE WARRINGTON LICENSING COURT.

Sir,—The following remarks are submitted with a view to assist in keeping alive the indignation that was aroused by the gross partiality and injustice which marked the proceedings of the local magistrates at the Tecent adjourned meeting of the Brewster Sessions. The case referred to, briefly stated, was this: Green- all, Whitley, and Co., already the owners of no less than 1194 rinking shops in Warrington alone, had for a long time past set their covetous eyes upon Catherine-st. and Battersby-lane. The first named street and others sur- rounding are mostly inhabited by the working classes, and they felt that if they could get an attractive and seductive gin palace set up there a large addition would be sure to be made to the grist which flows into their mill. Then Battersby-lane presented a singularly tempting field for their operations. In that locality there is a considerable working-class population, as yet comparatively free from the curse of the public-house ; an extensive Waggon Works, and the Infantry Barracks. A properly organised gin palace so favourably situated, would certainly develop " trade." Under its influence the cottagers would be demoralised ; no small portion of the wages paid at the Waggon Works, would find its way into the Greenall coffers, and the poor soldiers would spend their spare coppers in the fiery and inflam- ing poisons of the palace rather than in the watery stuff of the canteen. We need not wonder, then, that the owners of Wilderspool had set their hearts upon such desirable hunting grounds as these. But the tendency of these days is to reduce and not multiply facilities for drinking; and the astute traffickers in drunkenness knew that however much they might rely upon the " justices of Warrington to accommo- date them, it would be too barefaced even for Greenall- ism te approach their" worships" without some show of reason for the blessing which they so eagerly desired. And so they magnanimously offered to surrender a few licenses in congested districts if their" worships " would grant them permits to practice on the inhabitants of Catherine-st., and Battersby-lane ! A more brazen attempt to bamboozle a bench of magistrates, and turn the proceedings of a legal court into a contemptible farce was never before made even by Greenallism ! And now what was the position of their" worships," and how did they discharge their solemn duty to the public, whose servants they were to administer justice, and protect their interests from wroag doers? That they regarded the occasion as of great importance, was proved by the fact that no less than sixteen of them found time to attend the court. It sometimes happens, that justice has to be delayed in the same court, for lack of a magistrate, but on the occasion under review there was, from some secret cause or other, an abundant supply of thee" great unpaid." The majority of them were, of conrse, Tories, for the cases to be decided upon, con- cerned a great Tory firm, and as usual, where the carcase is, there the eagles are gathered together. The sameness of the Bench, however, was agreeably varied by the inclusion of a few Liberal w,irships, and a sprig or two of that remarkable political phenomenon known as " Liberal Unionism." The duty of the Bench, how- ever constituted, was without fear or favour to adminis ter the law as they found it, and the law, bad as it is, knows nothing of trucking between the Bench and the Publicans in the matter of granting or cancelling licenses.

Now it was admitted by the learned mouthpiece of the brewers, that there were far too many public-houses in some parts of the town, especially in Buttermarket- street, and every magistrate on the Bench knew from his own observation, that Greenallism had simply flooded that unfortunate locality. NVas it not then the plain and unmistakable duty of the magistrates, in the interests of public order, and the well being of the borough, to make a clean sweep of at least one halt of the drink shops, in Buttermarket-street, at any rate without any reference to or trucking about licenses in any other quarter ? Unfortunately for the town, their worships were not equal to the occasion. Instead of instantly and indignantly scouting the base and impu- dent proposition of the brewers, as an insult to them per- sonally, and a bold attempt to make the court a tcol for the furtherance of private interests, no less than eleven out of the sixteen magistrates present swallowed the bait presented, and granted two new licenses for districts where they are absolutely not required. Five of the Liberals on the Bench did not join in the verdict. The whole transaction from beginning to end, was scandalous, and an outrage on the working classes in the districts involved, who naturally look to the admit) istrators of the law, to protect them from evil doer. Had it been proposed to erect a gin palace in Palmyra Square, or some other fashionable quarter, how many of the eleven worships would have voted for it I But because some people are poor and unable to defend themselves, they must have the drink nuisances thrust upon them, whenever and wherever the liquor capital- ists find they can make good dividends out of their degradation and ruin. But where was " the Church "when this " Licensing job " was being enacted ? Where were Messrs. Willis, Jackson, Longhorn, &c., when the bounds of drunk- enness were being enlarged in this drink-ridden town of Warrington ? It suits their purpose occasionally to noseas temperance reformers in small mission rooms,and other obscure cc,rners, where a few poor 'Apple, looking upon them as oracles, can be induced to listen to their

orations against drunkenness, but not against the manufacturers of that destructive article. But when the tug of war comes,and some great and public effort is being made to reduce the number of public-houses," the clergy" are absolutely nowhere. And the reason is obvi- ous. Their disciple and friend, the great Liquor King of Wilderspool, is a great benefactor to " the Church." He loves their nation, and out of the gains of drunken- ness builds them a synagdgue now and then, and this is a kind of charity, which,•in the eyes of Warrington priests, covers a multitude of sins.—Yours &c., CITIZEN.

div.head: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
div.p: HARVEST FESTIVALS.
FESTIVALS ON THURSDAY EVENING.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held, on Thursday evening in St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath, St. Anne's, Warrington, and St. Barnabas's. The preacher at St. Thomas's was Canon McClure, Dean of Manchester, and the Rev. S. Wilkinson, of Timperley, occupied the pulpit at St. Anne's.

div.head: THEI:WALL.
div.p: THEI:WALL.

The first of the series of harvest festival services in connection with All Saints' Church, Thelwall, was held on Saturday evening, but owing, to doubt, to the un- favourable state of the weather, there was a small atten- dance. All Saints is now one of the prettiest churches in the country, with its charming windows and other adornments, and it looked particularly attractive on Saturday evening, a large quantity of fruit and flowers having been requisitioned for purposes of decoration. The Drder of service was as follows :—Processional hymn, 382 ; Magnificat and Nunc Dimittis, Langdon Colborne; Psalms cxlviii.-cl. ;lessons : first,Hosea ii. 14, second, St. John iv. 31-39 ; anthem, "Praise the Lord," Winchester; hymn, 384 anthem during the collection, "The Lord is loving unto every man," Garrett, Mug. D. ; recessional hymn, 305. For a village choir, the singing was excep- tionally good, and Mr. Cooke also demonstrated his skill in the manipulation of the organ. The solos in the first anthem were well rendered by Archie Taylor and Henry Scam In the absence of the Right Rev. Thomas Edward Wilkinson, Coadjutor-Bishop of London and of N. and E. Europe (who had been announced to preach), his sermon waa read by the Vicar, the Rev. T. Pym Williamson. The text was "That our eons may grow up as the young plants and that our daughters may be as the polished corners of the temple." The services were continued on Sunday. The offertories are to be divided between the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts and the Church of England Waifs':and Strays' Society.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, LATCEIFORD. The annual harvest thanksgiving services were held, at the above place of worship, on Sunday. The chapel was prettily decorated with corn, fruit, flowers, &c. Mr. S. Owen, of Widnes, preached both morning and evening. In the evening he preached to a large con- gregation from the words, "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." In the afternoon the choir rendered a Service of Song; entitled "Two autumn evenings," under the leadership of Mr. J. Massey. Mr. J. Griffith, superintendent of the Sunday School, read the connec- tive readings. Special hymns, appropriate to the occa- sion, were sung by the choir and congregation. Collec- tions were taken at the end of each service in aid of the trust fund. On Monday evening, an entertainment was held. In the unavoidable absence of Mr. E. Calvert of Widnes, Mr. J. Griffiths, assisted by the Rev. Mr. Thornley, took the chair. RecP•ations, songs, piccolo and clarionet solos were given by the following scholars and friends :—Messrs. 36. Critchley, A. Swarbrick, Jos. C oss, A. Adfield, Albert Tilley, and the Misses. Taylor, Littlewood, P. Rodgers, and E. Bredon. The choir sang several hymns during the evening,and Mr. Stanley Bridge proved himself an able accompanist. Fruit, &c., was distributed at intervals daring the evening, by Miss P. Lamb, H. Buckley, J. Stout, and A. and F. Mooney, under the charge of Mrs. Barber and Mrs. Adamson.

div.head: BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHAPEL.
div.p: BOLD-STREET WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with the Wesleyan Chapel, Bold-str t. were held on Sunday, special sermons being preached, in the morning by the Rev. J. Kirtlan (superintendent), and in the evening by the Rev. A. Freeman. In the morning the Rev. J. Kittlan based his discourse on the w Jrds " Oh give thanks unto the Lord, for He is good and His mercy endureth for ever." He spoke on the duty and privilege of gratitude in connection with the ingathering of the harvest. Mr. Freeman preached an appropriate sermon from the words : " Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground it abideth alone ; but if it die it bringeth forth much fruit." At Use morning service .the anthem, " What are these that are arrayed in white robes ?' (Sir J. Stainer) was very effectively rendered by the choir. I• 1 the evening the anthem was" Sing unto God with the voice of thanksgiving " (Edwyn A. Clare), the ' solo parts being very ably rendered by Mr. L. Richard- son. The duet" The Lard is my Shepherd" was taste- fully sung by Miss Gunton and Mr. L. Richardson. Mr. Peter Harrison was at the orgen. The music was one of the attractions of the service, there b3ing no decorations on account of the recent bazaar which was held in con- nection with the church. The collections, which realized a handsome total, are to be devoted to the cir- cuit funds.

div.head: SERVICES CONTINUED.
div.p: SERVICES CONTINUED.

The harvest —festival services in connection with St. Paul's and Holy Trinity Churches, lVarrington, were resumed on Sunday, when large congregations assembled, and appropriate hymns were sung. We have been requested to state that the anthem sung at St. Paul's Church on Thursday evening last (Sir John Stainer's "0 clap your hands ") was rendered by the choir, and the orchestral band simply accompanied. It was remark- ably well sung. PARISE anima WARRINGTON. The scene at the harvest festival at the Parish Church, Warrington, on Sunday was very impressive. To add to the general effect the church was decorated with the choicest flowers and fruits of the season. The preacher was the Rev. W. H. Cleaver, rector of Pulham St. Mary, Norfolk, and he based his sermon on Psalm cxxvi. Suitable harvest hymns were sung at each service dur- ing the day. PENKETH WESLEYA NS. .

The services in connection with the above were held in the Wesleyan Chapel, morning and evening. The Rev. Alfred Freeman preached both sermons. The chapel was neatly decorated with corn, fruit, vegetables, &c. A choice assortment of hot house plants also lent a charm to the scene. The services were fairly well 'attended,

div.head: WILLIAM CAREY, THE BAPTIST MISSIONARY.
div.p: WILLIAM CAREY, THE BAPTIST MISSIONARY.

- - On Sunday evening the Rev. John Yonge preached a sermon at Wycliffe Congregational Church, on "The great event of one hundred years ago to-day." lie commenced by saying that there was often a " Word of the Lord" distinct and unmistakable in history as really as in inspiration; in event as well as in Scripture. This became manifest not only in some striking occurrence which made a particular day mem- orable for ever ; but also in a chain or series of events which sprang from a known and definite source. Pre- eminently was this the case in the history of the Church of Jesus Christ. That day was the precise centenary of an event which had had probably larger influence upon the world and the human race than any one event that transpired since the Day of Pentecost. The year, 17, indeed, would ever b ; a year of conspicuous note in, at least, European history. It was the year of the great Revolution in France, when an oppress—l nation struck for liberty against tyranny and oppression, and kings and courts trembled all over Europe. But the event he had to speak of that night,revolutionary though it was in essential character, was of far greater conse- quence to mankind. It might probably be overlooked, and unrecorded -by any human recorder of the world's history, but they might be conadent that the Recording Angel of God had inscribed the occurrence upon the infallible annals of time, as one of the ruling events in the providential and redemptive government of man- kind. On October 2nd, 1792, William Carey, shoe- maker, schoolmaster, and minister, with twelve friends, assembled at Kettering, and" solemnly agreed to act in society together " for the propagation of the gospel among the heathen. That was the event. Its scene was a little back parlour in a private house, the hour was after the services of a busy Sabbath. The actors were 12 or 13 ministers of the Baptist persuasion. Mr. Yonge described how this meeting led three years later to the formation of the London Missionary Society. The prime instigator of the Baptist missionary enterprise, William Carey, eventually became the first and famous missionary in it. The rev, gentleman gave a review of Carey's life, mentioning that "Cook voyages round the world" was the book that helped to make a missionary of him, and after recounting the results throughout the world, of the work originated by him, claimed that they were a clear proof that God's blessing was on them.

div.head: TALE OF A DONKEY.
div.p: A TALE OF A DONKEY.

At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guar- dians, on Wednesday, Mr. W. Houghton, said that someone had turned a donkey ont to graze on the lawn at Padgate Industrial Schools. He did not know whether it had been sent as an ornament to the landscape, to pick up an industrial training, or to teach music. (Laughter.) Ho thought the animal would do damage to the shrubs and plants and the beds and bor- ders. He was told that a member of the Board had sent it there, but whether he had turned it out on the lawn or that was done by the superintendent he cmuld not say. The Clerk (Mr. J. C. Sutton) pointed out that the law of impounding still prevailed in country districts. Mr. Muir thought that Mr. Houghton had begun at the wrong end of the stick. He should have told them to begin with, that there was an understanding between the surerintendent and the donkey. (Laughter.) The Chairman (Mr. R. Heaton) said he should put the donkey in a stable, and if it were not claimed within a certain time he should sell it to clear expenses. The Clerk said he would write to the superintendent to say that no donkey would be allowed on the school premises. (Laughter.) Mr. Gill : I hope that won't be personal. The Clerk said he could put in the proviso no" four- legged" donkey. (Laughter.) The subject then dropped.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 8, 1892.

div.head: DEA.TH OF MR. GEORGE SHEFFIELD.
div.p: DEA.TH OF MR. GEORGE SHEFFIELD.

We regret to record the death of Mr. George Sheffield, the artist, so well-known in this district from his long connection with Warrington. He was 53 years of age, and leaves a large family unprovided for; his with died some years ago. Ile was not a native of Warrington, though he received his early training in art in the town. He was of Cumberland origin, having been born at Wigton, on the Ist January, 1839. As a mere child he came to Lancashire with his parents, settled at Warrington, and afterwards in Manchester, receiving his training in art first at Warrington and subsequently at the Manchester School of Art. At first he proposed for himself the profession of a pattern designer to calico printers. As a designer Sheffield showed originality and power, aim might have dene work of the first rate had he remained in that occupation. But when a few small delicately executed water-colour drawings, mostly local landscapes, found ready purchasers he decided to devote all his attention to pictorial art. About 1865 he left Manchester for the neighbourhood of Bettwys-y-Coed. Here he painted from morning to night, constantly finding new subjects in the picturesque valleys of the Lledr, the Llugwy, and the Conway. His work at that period was much admired by artistsand amateurs then sojourning at Bettws. Among his earliest works of note ex- hibited were some three or four drawings sent from that happy hunting ground of artists to the Royal Institution Autumn Exhibition in 1868. Two of these attracted particularly favourable notice—one a drawing of that mass of solitary grandeur Llyn Idwal, the other a delicately executed picture of the well-known Fairy Pool on the Conway. At ' the next year's exhibition (1869) he was even better represented, and in this year Sheffield was elected an associate of the Manchester Academy, being elected a full member in 1871. About this period he took up his residence at Wilmslow,and be- gan that long series of drawings in black and white by which he made his name. Having a strong love of the sea,he:on:severalloccasions joined as one of the creve,of ship 3 bound to America and other distant ports. Among his best sea paintings may be mentioned the "Passing Storm—Holland" and "The Scheldt," exhibited in 1875 and " Bunbeg, Bar, Coast of Donegal," exhibited in 1876. He was extremely rapid in his execution. At the Jubilee Exhibition at Old Trafford he was capitally represented by a water-colour drawing, "Near Douglas, Isle of Man.' He produced a very large number of water-colour drawings, and exhibited several note- worthy works in oil. One of the latter, "A Hundred Years Ago," exhibited in 1890, was purchased by the Manchester Corporation, and now hangs in the perman- ent collection in the City Art Gallery. The deceased was well known in Warrington, and his death will be regretted by the scores of friends he had made in the town. The opening conversazione of the winter session of the Manchester Literary Club was held on Monday evening, round the wails of the room being pictures by the late Mr. Christopher Blacklock, Mr. Frederick Shields. and the late Mr. George Sheffield. Mr. George Milner gave a brief address in the course of the proceedings. They had, he said, heard that afternoon of the death of Mr. George Sheffield. They were not taken by surprise, but they were none the less saddened by the news. Mr. Milner pointed to 11 pictures and sketches on the wall dtawn by Mr. Sheffield. A large picture, drawn in the early days of the artist and given by him to the club, was marvellous in its execution. Some of the other pictures shown were drawings made in the club in the course of 7i minutes. He thought no man had a clearer idea of what it was possible to do in black and white, or greater facility for putt:ng his ideas on paper qr on can- vas than George Sheffield. They could not help regret- ting that he did not execute more works of the very fine nullity of the one he presented to the club many years ago. SHEFFIELD AS AN 91ITIST.

BY ONE WHO KNEW HIM. Sheffield was a genius, if over there was one. For he had something more than " infinite capacity for taking pains "—that is when it suited him to do so. He had a powerful imagination, and an express faculty for depict- ing what he saw. I have seen him, when in the humour for doing a black and white drawing, hesitate for two or three minutes as to whether it should be a landscape or a seascape, and then, having decided, after forming a picture in his mind, set to work with a sort of" divine fury," to body forth his conception. One of the finest black and white drawings he ever executed was pre- sented to his friend Mr. Birtles, photographer, and was acco.nplished, without a single pause, in an hour and seven minutes. On other occasions he has dashed off smaller and less important work in half the time. It will be remembered that he executed a large black and white drawing as an infirmary contribution, some few years ago. It was begun and finished in the dining room of Mr. Thomas Morris, as a sort of object lesson, in the presence of a score of guests, who were invited to wit- ness the performance. The friends about him were chat- ting and smoking, and he did the same at intervals, finishing the drawing in about two hours and a half. It sold, it may be added, for something over £lO. It was something more than a theory with Sheffield that the medi.im was a matter of little moment to the genuine artist ; and he demonstrated his view by the marvellous facility with which he could turn from oil to water colours, and from crayons to charcoal. I was present on one occasion when, by way of illustrating a method of working, he got a little soot from the back of the chimney, rubbed some of it on paper with his fingers, took out his pocket knife, began scratching with it,and, without any other aid, finished a powerful little sketch within a quarter of an hour. There can be no question that he would have occupied one of the highest positions in the realm of art if it had not been for his one great failing, his fondness for the glass. It is a thousand pities that it should have been so, and yet it is but the simple truth to say that his almost chronic im- pecuniosity caused him to execute hundreds, indeed, I may say thousands, of "black and white"—good and bad—that would Otherwise have never had an existence. His own humorous way of putting it was that it was God's way of getting work out of him. The following lines, which were written for the " Examiner" when the artist was living in Warrington in 1885, will doubt- less be read with renewed interest at the present mo- ment :

------ - George Sheffield's a wonderful man— A wonderful artist is he ; With his seeing eye and his cunning hand, He will make you picture of sea or of land— Of ship, or tower, or tree. He's at home on the roaring main, _ _ .

, When the loud winds lasr; the deep ; He will paint you this, o.nd then, again, He will show you the sea ene great, smooth plain As calm as a child asleep. It is now a country scene— A river glowing and bright, With clumps of trees and a church between ; It is now a tale of what has been—

A castle stormed in the nigh t. In colour, or " black and white," He has ever a marvellous touch ; I've seen him lay " soot " on as black as night, And instantly turn it to clear moonlight— He once made a picture with " slutch." He's a comet amongst his kind—
A spurner of bolts and bars, And whenever he leaves this earth behind. You will find he has mounted the wings of the wind To go paintit.g amid the stars.

div.head: CIGAR ENDS FOR WARRINGTON PAUPERS.
div.p: CIGAR ENDS FOR WARRINGTON PAUPERS.

At Warrington Board of Guardians, the Work- house Master (Mr. Ward), reported that parcels of fruit had been sent for the inmates, from Holy Trinity and St. Paul's Churches, from St. Mary's, Great Sankey,per Mr. !V'. P. Skelton. and a parcel of tobacco from Mr. Pritchard, Horsemarket-street, per Mr. A. Jolley. Mr. Gill asked what this gift of tobacco consisted of? The Workhouse Master : A box of cigar ends. Mr. Gill said he had heard that it was 51 in the town, and a more *gusting present could hardly be given to paupers or anyone else. He understood they were collected from public-heuses. (No, no, and hear, hear.) Those cigar ends were cellected from public-houses; he believed that was so. They were collected after they had been In the mouth of nobody knew whom ; they were saved for a certain time to dry and then they were sent to the Workhouse as" presents." He should move that it be an instruction to the Work- house Master never to let the inmates use cigar ends in the future. If they had to have tobacco let it be decent tobacco. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Shaw seconded this pro- posal. The Workhouse Master said some of the cigar ends had been smoked. Mr. Muir thought the question was whether the inmates were satisfied or not. Mr. A. Jolley said he got some of the cigar ends from Mr. Toft the tobacconist. Mr. Shaw said he had no doubt it had all been done with good intentions. But if the gift consisted of fresh cigar ends from Mr. Tuft his name ought to be given. Mr. Gill's motion on being put to the meeting was voted for by seven members, and none held up their hands against it. .It was, however, rule] that as seven was not a majority of the Board the motion was not carried. The Clerk said it would no doubt be understood that cigar ends that had been used were not to be given to the inmates. Mr. Jolley said ho would send no more of those. The Clerk remarked that everybody would give Mr. Jolley credit tor good infßintiorui.
DEATH OF TENNYSON.
The following was posted at the gate entrance to Aldsworth house on Thursday morning : " Lord Tennyson passed away quite peacefully at 1.35 a.m. (Signed) .
" ANDREW CLARK. "G. H. R. DABBS,"

A correspondent at Huse'mere, Surrey, telegraph- ing, says :—The end of Lord Tennyson was eminently peaceful. There was not the slightest trace of suffering to distress his sorrowing relatives and friends, and once or twice during the night he smiled upon those watching at his bedside. When the end came he appeared as one in sleAp, and so restful was the close of his life that those around him scarcely knew when he had pmmsed away. SIR A. CLARKE'S ACCOUNT.

The special corremmdent of the Central News says: —Although Lord Tennyson died in the early hours the information was not made known to anyone outside the household for a long time afterwards. All the members of the family were with him at the time I had a short interview with Sir Andrc N Clarke this morning before his departure from flaslemere for London. The distin- guished physician said," Lord Tennyson has had a glori- ously beautiful death. In all my experience I have never witnessed anything more glorious. There were no artificial lights in the chamber, and all was in dark- ness, save for the silvery Pliit of the moon at its full. The soft beams of light fell upon the bed and played • upon the features of the dying poet like a halo of Rem- brandt's." The bedside was watched from Wednesday morning until the moment of death by the physicians, and also by the Hon. Hallam Tennyson, the poet's son. The scene at the close was highly affecting. The news of her husband's death was gently broken to Lady Tennyson, who, despite her delicate state of health, bore the news of her bereavement with fortitude. Sir Andrew Clarke left Flaslemere for London by the 8.26 train. LORD TENNYSON'S PERSONALTY.

The personalty of Tennyson, says a London corres- pondent, was unknown to the general public, owing to his having with increased care and energy, as age ad- vanced, shut himself up in the privacy of his house and grounds. It was characteristic of the traditions of the house to read how the gate giving entrance to the grounds of Aldworth House has been jealously fastened with a strong rope, a basket being provided for persons who will leave cards or friendly messages. Yet up to a very recent time Tennyson was accessible to intimate friends or to persons recommended to him under pecu- liar circumstances. Four years ago he had an at- tack of illness, from which he never fully recovered. It was so serious that he was induced to give up smoking—an abstention which did not last long. Some years ago an attempt was made by a connection of the Poet Laureate to claim heirship to the Barony of D'Eyncourt. There was some, but not much, foundation for this. Tennyson, like Shakspeare, sprang from the people. His great grandfather was Richard Tennyson, apothecary, of Stainton, Lincoln- shire. He married the daughter of an alderman of .1 Grimsby, who claimed lineal descent from the D Eyncourt tree. It is understood that Lord Tennyson was in receipt of a handsome income from the copyright of his works. When Messrs. Strahan and Co.' became his publishers they paid him £5OOO down for his books then in existence, with a separate account for new works. For five years this contract ran, and Messrs. Strahan's books, I believe, show that in that time they paid him an aggregate sum of £31,000. His next pub- lishers were King and Co., who undertook to pay him £4,000 a year, with a separate account for new works. Lord Tennyson at one time made a practice of running up to London at least once a year. and roaming about, as far as possible, unrecognised. But no one could pass him without turning to look at one of the strangest figures that ever trod the streets of modern London— , a tall, round-shouldered man. Growing stout in these later years, he always walked with a stick, and gave the impression that he was not entirely free from gout. A long beard covered his face, and he looked out through a pair of large spectacles upon a world which, on the whole.' he was rather inclined to despise. In supplement of his spectacles there dangled across the somewhat shabby- looking tweed dustcoat, a pair of geld-rimmed eyeglasses. The tweed dustcoat, in colour a rusty red, was evidently an acquaintance of many years, and had now grown too tight for him across the chest, over which it was neverthele•s determinedly buttoned. Dark trousers with gaiters over his thick-soled boots, and a broad-brimmed hat, probably older by some years than the tweed dust- coat, completed the dress of the Poet Laureate when last he was seen sturdily plodding. across Regent's Park. MEMOIR OF THE POET. Alfred Tennyson, D.C.L., F.R.S., Poet Laureate, third son of the late R. I. C. Tennyson, the elder brother of the Right Hon. C. Tennygon D'Eyncourt, was born its 1809, at his father's parsonage, at Somerby, Lincoln- shire, his mother, who died in 1885, being a daughter of the Rev. Stephen Fytche. He was educated by his father, and in due course proceeded to Trinity College, Carnbt idge. In 1829 he gained the Chancellor's Medal by a poem in blank verse, entitled " Timbuctoo." With the exception of a volume of poems published in con- junction with his brother Charles, when they were boys, and a prize poem, composed whilst an undergraduate , at Cambridge, Mr. Tennyson did not publish any- I thing till 1830, when " Poems chiefly Lyrical" ap- peared, and from 1842 the steady and rapid growth of his fame may be traced. The two volumes then issued were in part merely a republication, but the most important poems were those added to his former productions, It was at once apparent that the author of the " Mort d'Arthur," " Locicsley Hall," the " May Queen," and the "Two Voices" was entitled to the first rank among English poets, a reputation which was more than sus- tained by the two great works which followed. So well known and popular, indeed, had Mr. Tennyson become after the publication of " In Memoriam," in 1850, that it seemed only a " matter of course," upon the death of Wordsworth, in 1851, that the privilege of wearing " the laurel greener from the brows of him who uttered nothing base" should be offered to him. The " Ode on the death of the Duke of Wellington " was published in 1852, on the morning of the funeral ; and since that occurence few events of more than ordinary interest in the eyes of Englishmen have taken place without elicit- ing from the Laureate some poem worthy of the occasion. He has written " Poems chiefly Lyrical," published in 1830 ; " Poems," in 1832; " Poeme."2 vols. In 1842; " The Princess, a Medley," in 1847; "In Memoriam," issued anonymously. in 1850, being a series of elegies—a tribute of affection to the memory of Arthur Hallam a son if the eminent historian, and the chosen friend ohhe poet in his earlier days at Cambridge; "Maude, and other Poems," in 1855 ; " The Idylls of the King," in 1858 •, " Enoch Arden, and other Poems," in 1884 ; "The Holy Grail, and other Poems," published December 15, 1869 "The Window, or the Songs of the Wrens," in 1870; and " Gareth and Lynette." in 1872. "A Concordance to the entire Works of Alfred Tennyson," published in 1869, is a remarkable proof of the Laureate's wondrous popul- arity. At the commemoration of 1855 the University of Oxford, giving expression to the universal feeling of England, conferred on the poet the honorary degree of D.C.L., and the fellows of his own college, Trinity, Cambridge, endorsing the judgment of the sister univer- sity, subscribed to purchase his best (by Woolner), which they have Placed in the vestibule of their library, and in 1869 they unanimously elected him an honorary fellow of the college. In 1879 Mr. Tenny- son republished "The Lover's Tale," a poem which was originally printed in 1833, tut soon withdrawn from circulation. In the reissue it is accompanied with a reprint of the sequel, a work of the author's mature life. "The Golden Supper." Among his dramatic composi- tihns are, " Queen Mary," 1875 ; " Harold," 1876: "The Cup," a play which was represented at the Lyce- um Theatre, January 3, 1881, Mr. Irving taking the principal character ,• and "The Promise of May," a drama in three ne"s, brought out at the Globe Theatre, November 11, 1882. In December, 1883, Mr. Tennyson accepted the dignity of a baron of the United Kingdom, assuming the title of Lord Tennyson. A new volume of poems from Lord Tennyson heads Messrs. Macmillan and Co.'s long and promising list of forthcoming books. The title announced is" Akbar's Dreams and other Poems." THE NEW BARON TENNYSON.

Lord Tennyson is succeeded in the -title by big son ,the Bon. Hallam Tennyson, who, in 1884, married Audrey, daughter of the late Mr. Charles John Boyle, and has two sons, Lionel Hallam, born in 1889, and Alfred Aubrey, born in 1891. TELEGRAMS OF CONDOLENCE. MESSAGE FROM THE QUEEN.

The news of the poet's death was telegraphed to the Queen about nine o'clock yesterday morning, and in little over an hour a touchingly-worded telegram of sympathy was received from her Majesty. During the day many other telegrams of condolence were received, including messages from the Prince ot Wales and Mr. Gladstone ; but there were few callers at Aldworth House. INTERMENT' IN WESTMINSTER ABBEY. The remains of Lord Tennyson will be buried in West- minster Abbey on Wednesday afternoon next, in the grave adjoining that of Robert Browning. The inner shell of Lord Tennyson's coffin arrived at Ilaslemere from London at eleven o'clock on Friday morning. The outer oak case will follow on Monday next. The in- scription on the coffin will be simply "Alfred, Lord Tennyson," with the date of birth and death.

THE POET-LAUREATESHIP. The office of Poet Laureate is one of great antiquity in the household of the Sovereigns of Great Britain, the appellation having its origin in a custom of the English universities, which was continued until 1512, of present- ing a laurel leaf to graduates in rhetoric and versifica- tion, the King's " laureate " being a graduated rhetori- cian in the service ef the King. One of the duties of the poet laureate was to write an ode in celebration of the birthday of the monarch, but this custom was discon- tinued after the reign of George 111. The distinction is now purely honorary. A salary of £lOO is, however, attached to the office with an additional sum of £27, in lieu of a tierce of Canary wine, which was formerly (since the reign of Charles I.) granted to the poet annu- ally. A VISIT TO THE DEATH CHAMBER.

A special correspondent of the Press Association gives an account of a visit to the Poet Laureate's death cham- ber. As he reclines lifeless upon his bed Lord Tennyson Looks some LE years younger than before death, the lines and wrinkles having passed from the face, while the beard, unkempt enough in life, is carefully brushed and trimmed. The hands are folded over the chest, a lauroal wreath crowns the head, and another reposes at the feet. Flowers, principally Virginia creepers, almost hide the coverlet from view. Wax tapers supply a subdued light to the death chamber, which is wrapped in solemn silence.

div.head: WARRIN,GTON TECHNICAL [NSfITUTE.
div.p: WARRIN,GTON TECHNICAL [NSfITUTE.

It is much to be regretted that the classes in connec- tion with this Institute are not being filled up so readily as might have been expected. In all abAut 200 students have joined, but that is only about a third of the num- ber who joined last year. Among the special means I adopted by the committee of the Institute to popularize! its classes is the offer of fifteen free scholarships to the value of 10s. each, tenable at the Institute's classes dur- ing the session of 1892-3. These scholarships are open to boys or girls who have left or are leaving Elementary Day Schools in the borough during the year 1892. On Tuesday thirteen of the scholarships were awarded, the committee, having, 0: course, reserved the right to withhold any of the scholarships in the event of an in- sufficient number of candidates presenting themselves. There were forty-thres candidates, and the names of the thirteen successful ones are as follows :—Charlie Eforo- bin, Mary E. Hudson, Edith Chidlaw, Laura Norman, 'Gertrude Bramhall, Walter A. Clay, Wm. R. Blease, Frederick Webster, Walter Bond, Wilfrid Rigby, Fredk. IJ. Robinson, Margaret Womersley. and Herbert C. Cooper. The young people may attend as many as three different classes during the session free of cost.

The committee of the Warrington Co-operative Society are also issuing a circular to their members. calling attention to the classes and pointing out the value of the knowledge that is to be acquired by attending them. To give practical expression to their view, the committee propose to offer to nay the class fe(s to an amount not exceeding six shillings each of, say, 51 students being members, or sons or daughters of members, of the society, not more than one person from each family being eligible. If more than 50 applications are received that number will be chosen by ballot.

div.head: SCHOOL OF ART VACATION SKETCHING CLUB.
div.p: THE SCHOOL OF ART VACATION SKETCHING CLUB.

The annual adjudication- of prizes for work done, during the vacation has just been made by Mr. J. B. Gibbs, of Liverpool, who expressed himself as well satisfied with the character of the work submitted. The prizes were awarded as follows :—General competi- tion : Advanced section, first, Miss Kerry; second, 0. Garside; third, Miss M. Burgess. Elementary section : first, Miss K. Brundrett ; second, Miss Woods; third, Miss E. Swanwick. Special competition :I. (study from life), Mr. Rylands's prize, Miss A. Chrimes ; second, 0. Garside. 11. (study of flowers) Mr. Garnett's prize, John Millard; highly commended, Miss Chrimes, Miss Kerry. 111. (set of sketches in black and white), Mr. Birtles's prize, Miss Kerry; highly commended, C. E. Jones. VI. (set of architectural sketches), C. E. Jones; highly commended, 0. Garside. VIII. (outdoor study from nature), Miss M. Burgess.

div.head: PROPOSED WARRINGTON DOCKS.
div.p: THE PROPOSED WARRINGTON DOCKS.

We understand that a movement has been set on foot by certain local gentlemen interested in the matter, to push forward as far as possible, the con- struction of the Warrington docks. The Ship Canal Company have already been approached on the sub- ject. We hope to be in a position to give further information before long.

DIED WHILST AT PRAYER AT WIDNES. The Widnes police on Monday, notified Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, of the death of a hawker named Mary Kilmartin, a widow, sixty-five years of age, lodging at 12, Moss-street, Moss Bank, Wid- nes, which occurred early on Sunday morning under somewhat extraordinary circumstances. It appears that the woman with whom deceased lodged (Mrs. Connington) left deceased about eleven o'clock en Satur- day night kneeling on a wooden sofa, saying her prayers About four o'clock yesterday morning Mr. Connington, who is employed at one of the Widnes cheep ical works, came home, and then he found the deceased in the same posture as his wife had left her in five hours pre- viously. He did not receive any answer when he called the woman, and then he discovered that she was dead. The deceased, it appears, had suffered from bronchitis and asthma for many years. The Coroner deems an inquest unnecessary.

PE SHIP CANAL. A SUDDEN DEATH. On Monday morning Mr. J. E. Worsley held an inquest on the body of George Brown, 45 years of age, labourer on the Manchester Ship Canal works' at Norton, in the mission-room, Big Field. Mrs. Goodwin, with whom the deceased had lodged, spoke to him going out about two o'clock on Thursday afternoon: Ile returned be- tween six and seven o'clock the same night. Later, Elizabeth Beckington, servant, on going to the closet, found him in a sitting posture dead. The body was removed to the mission-room. A verdict of died from natural causes was recorded. BOILER EXPLOSION NEAR FRODSLIAM.—FIVE

MEN INJURED. On Monday, another disaster occurred on the Man- chester Ship Canal, and although the accident was not so serious as at first reported (no lives having been lost), ' five workmen were injured—two very seriously. The cause of the accident was the explosion of the boiler of a locomotive at the works on Frodsham Marsh, five or six miles from Runcorn, It appears that about eleven o'clock on Monday morning one of the company's loco- motives, named the Kenyon, was leaving the locomotive shed at Frodsham Marsh. The engine had been lying up for some time undergoing certain repairs, and it left the shed on Monday morning at the time stated on a sort of trial trip. The locomotive was in charge of its usual driver, a man named Roberts, and the foreman fitter and a youth named Neil were also on it when it left the shed. The engine had not proceeeed many yards when one of the plates of the fire box by rst. The foreman litter was on the foot plate, and he was badly hurt, his right side and leg being injured it is supposed by the door of tho stokehole being blown away and catching him in its flight. The driver Roberts was very badly scalded about the head and arms, but the youth Neil was the most seriously injured. He sustained very serious scalds about the head, arms, aad upperparts of the body, and is in a rather precarious condition. He is about 18 years of age. Two fitters' labourers who happended to be standing near the lo3omotive when the explosion oc- curred, were also rather seriously scalded, one about the head and arms, and the other about the upper part of the body. Two of the injured men were removed to the company's hospi al at Latchford, near Warrington, but the three other workmen whose injuries were not of so serious nature were removed to their respective homes. , The man Wilson and the boy Neil are progressing ' favourably in the company's hospital at Latchford. Neil's condition is the more critical of the two, his eyes in particular beina badly scalded.

div.head: – THE BURTONWOOD ASSAULT.
div.p: - THE BURTONWOOD ASSAULT.

THE VICTIM STILL SUFFERING. At the Occasional Court, Warrington, on Monday, before Major Pickmere, a man named Dutton was charged on remand with assaulting another man on a Saturday night some time ago near the Limerick Hotel, Burtonwood. It was stated that the injured man was still unable to appear, and the case was accordingly remanded until October 19.—1 t v-ill be remembered that at the first hearing of the charge it was stated that Dutton and another man met near the Limerick Hotel on a Saturday night. Some words ensued as to work. Words led to blows and a struggle ensued, in which it is alleged that Dutton seized a spade which the injured men was carrying and struck him to the ground. The assaulted man was discovered an hour afterwards lying on the road with his leg broken and otherwise injured. He was conveyed to the hotel, where medical assistance was procured. The man was afterwards conveyed home where he now lies. SHOCKING MURDER IN IRELAND.

On Saturday morning the Carrick on Suir police arrested an agricultural labaurer named Doyle, on a charge of murdering Edward Quinlan, a farmer, of Ballinderry, county Tipperary. From evidence given at the inquest on Saturday, it appeared that Doyle was in Quinlan's employment, and that they had a dispute in the kitchen of the farmhouse, where they struck each other. Doyle then left the house and returned with a heavy stick, with which he fractured Quinlan's skull whilst the latter was reading a newspaper. Doyle escaped, and (luring a dark night he crossed the Suir, and reaching the County Waterford side of the river he secreted himself in :he thickly planted wood of Collima- muck, where after two nights' disappearance, he was lying in a hole he had dug, and covered with shrubbery.

div.head: SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC
div.p: THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC
AT WARRINGTON.

There has during the past week been a considerable addition to the number of smallpox cases in Warrington. At the end of last week there had been a total of 118 cases since the 28th of July ; yesterday, according to the report of the medical officer, the total had risen to 147 cases, thus showing au increase of 29 for the week. At the end of last week there had been six deaths,there have , now been nine. One of the three deaths of this week is that of another member of the family of the late Mr. Lawless, fishmonger, a youth 19 years of age. Scarlet fever is also still very prevalent in the town, and with regard to it the following statement has been issued : " Health Department, Town Hall, Warrington, 7th October, 1892. Scarlet fever. Various statements from irresponsible persons have been made with respect to the closing of schools in consequence of the preval- ence of this disease. At present there is no necessity as the medical officer of health is able to take every case notified into hospital, and especially if notified early to prevent further extension in the family. There are at present 77 cases in the hospital." The following statement has also been issued with regard to smallpox: Hope Hospital, Dallam-lane, Warrington, October 7th, 1892. Cases notified since 28th July Total number of deaths 9
Admitted to Hope Hospital since 19th Sept. 111 Discharged cured _ . _
Dead 5 At present in Hospital 97 JOHN GUEST GORNALL, Medical Superintendent. MORE ROOM WANTED AT THE HOPE HOSPITAL.

Dr. John Gornall, who has been appointed to assist his father, the medical officer of health, com- menced his duties by entering the Hope hospital on Tuesday night, and attending upon the patiencs. The additional rooms which have been provided in the front part of the works have been made use of this week for the accommodation of convalescent patients, and as it is very necessary that they should have separate accomodation, and as, too, there is little or no prospect of a decline of the out- break, the necessity for another room has already become apparent. A difficulty that has now to be inet is that workmen are natural:y reluctant to enter parts of the building already occupied by patients, with a view to making this further pro- vision, and unless this reluctance can be overcome there is reason to fear an aggravation of the crisis, which is already a serious one. When the rooms now occupied by convalescents were being got ready the workmen were separated by the length of the works from the patients, but in case of fur- ther preparation they would be in pretty close con- tact with the convalescents.

FLUTTERING THE SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. We learn that there was a pretty large attendance at the School Attendance Committee, on Thursday, of people who had been summoned to appear before the Committee for neglecting to send their children to schoal. It transpired that amongst the number was a woman who had come directly from a house where smallpox had been raging, and there was a disposition to reprimand her for coming there and staying so long to wait her turn amongst other people,but she naturally retotted that, as she was summoned to attend, she did not see low she could avoid it. It is hardly necessary to say that the Committee disposed of her case as soon as possible and permitted her to go home.

div.head: OUTBREAK AT ANPROBUS.
div.p: OUTBREAK AT ANPROBUS.

At the meeting on Tuesday of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, the Medical Officer presented the fdllowing report :—I have to report that an outbreak of smallpox has occurred at Antrobus. Two cases have occurred. The outbreak has arisen from Warrington, wt are smallpox is at present epidemic. The patients were children of parents who are at present in the Smallpox ficspital, Warrington, and the children were removed to Antrobus, owing to their Warrington home .ing temporarily closed. They developed the disease three days after arrival in Antro'ous, It is very gratify- ing to be able to report that Dr. Gornall, medical officer of health for Warrington, has removed these cases to Warrington Smallpox Hospital, but this outbreak once more serves to remind this Authority of the need of an infectious diseases hospital being erected, which I have steadily recommended since I have had the honour of being your medical officer of health.—A discussion fol- lowed, in which Mr. Heywood said they had this matter to face every time an outbreak occurred.—The Medical Mier said a hospital might be erected for a cost of £Z,OOO, which would be spread over 36 townships, and if the charge were spread over thirty years, the annual lepayment of principal and interest would amount to very little.—Mr. Brandreth said it was not long. ago , they had to pay £l7 for removing from Norton to War- rington, a patient suffering from scarlet fever. If other cases of smallpox had to be removed to Warrington the probable cost would be 24 guineas each.—On the pro- position of Mr. Heywood, seconded by Mr. Williams, a committee was appointed to consider the question of erecting a hospital, and report to the next meeting. The Committee consists of Messrs. Mclntyre, Knowles, Parr, Smith, Stokes, Jno. Whitlow, and Aaron. iIBALTH AND WEATHER, OF WAURINUTON.

For week ending Saturday, Oct. let, 1892, which was the 39th of the cutrent year, the following births and deaths were registered :—Births : War- rington, 34; Latchford, 5; total 39. Deaths: War- rington, 18; Latchford, 2; total 20. The excess of births over deaths was 19. The death-rate feom all causes was equal to 192 per 1,000 against 21.8 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 22.5 the corresponding week of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 2.8 per 1,000, against 6.4, the average rate of the four previous weeks, alid against 5.9 the corresponding week of 1891. The ages of mortality, were- 0 to 1 6; 1 to 5,4; 5 to 15, 2; 15 to 25, 0; 25 to 60,7 ; 60 upwards, 1; total 20. The deaths included-2 from smallpox, 1 from diarrhcea, 1 from acute rheumatism, 2 from phthisis,4 from lung disease, 2 from brain disease, 1 from heart disease, 4 from diseases of stomach, 1 from kidney disease. The follcwing cases of infectious disease have been reported during the week : Smallpox 20, scarlet fever 25, diphtheria 1, enteric fever 2. Meteorology.—The mean temperature was 52 Fah., and therefore 21 degree colder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature, 64 F., was recorded on the 24th inst., and the tninimlin temperature 40 F., on the Ist inst. The rainfall measured 1.58 in. The general direction of the wind was S.W., the reading of the Anemometer denoting 1565 miles.—JoHN H. GORIsTALL, Medical Officer of Health.

div.head: ANOTHER LAMP FATALITY.
div.p: ANOTHER LAMP FATALITY.

--- The Blackburn Coroner yesterday morning received information of a shocking paraffin lamp fatality. A painter, named Kennedy, living at Or": Darwen, was clearing his supper wife, who hwohheand I.l..euaubp;eatt haerbburrenaisnt.g paraffin lamp. n attempted to save a shawl will; caught fire, and mother and child were instantly enveloped in flames. Both were taken to the infirmary where the baby quickly succumbed, and the mother lies in a pecarious condition.

div.head: SAILORS POISONED AT SEA
div.p: SAILORS POISONED AT SEA

-- Seven of the crew of the British steamer Yorker,. which has arrived at Marseilles from Rangoon,died from poisoning shortly after leaving Perim. They had all eaten of fish taken on the East African coast.
A WOOLWICH TRA_GEDY.

On Saturday afternoon a waterman named John . Armitage shot a married woman named Frances Per kins, at Sellwater Gate, Woolwich, and then shot him- self. The weapon used was a revolver. Jealousy is assigned as the motive. The womah lies in a precari- ous state.
• MURDER OF A WOMAN AT BRISTOL

The county magistrates at Bristol on Monday com- mitted for trial Albert Manning, who is charged with the murder of a married woman named Flew, with whom he had lived whilst separated from his wife. Evidence of fierce jealousy on the prisoner's part was given, and of the fact that he had admitted firing at the woman. had previously previously made a rough will.

ARRIVAL OF THE NEW LORD-, LIEUTENANT. Lord Houghton, Irish Viceroy, made his entry into - Dublin on Monday afternoon, and was accorded. a favourable reception. He travelled on Sunday eveTng from London to Holyhead, and remained there all mg" leaving on Monday morning by special steamer, which arrived at Kingstown about twelve o'clock. Upon dis- embarkation a Royal salute was fired, and the band played the National Anthem. A special train conveyed the viceregal party to Westland-row Station, when tbs Viceroy rode to the Castle. The route of the procession was guarded by military.

div.head: MURDER AT ASHTON-UNDER-LYNE..
div.p: MURDER AT ASHTON-UNDER-LYNE..

-- The remains of George Percival, who is sup Posed er' have been murdered at Ashton-under-Lyne on the 2ath ult., were exhumed on Tuesday, and as a result of the post-mortem examination, made on WednesdaY, •t" men, named James dlcock and Richard Swan, have been arrested. They are charged with murdering Cie°rge Percival, who was found dead near Ashton-under-Lyno and was supposed to have been killed by falling from the top of a haystack. At Ashton Police Court, 00 Thursday, when the prisoners were brought up, evideneci was given of cries of " Murder !" haying been hear., near the place where Percival's body was discovered, and the sister of one of the prisoners handed to the Police a handkerchief which she bad received from her brother,- and which was alleged to have belonged to the deceased. The prisoners were remanded.

That night be decided, and the die V 71113 cast; whether for weal or woe only Heaven knew, Arthur had decided on the morrow to ask Elaine to he his wife. He saw her standing alone in the breakfast-mom when he entered; the wan, white face struck him at once. "Elaine," he said, approaching her, "have they told you that I will not be ready for this out-going steamer, and my trip mast necessarily be delayed a little ? I cannot get off to-day." She raised her eyes to his. "If it is not to-day, it will be to-morrow, or tbe day after—or the day will soon come when you will go." He drew nearer her, and took the little hand that was toying with the green leaves of the magnolia blossoms." "I have something to ask you first, Elaine," be. said. "Come into the drawing-room with me; 1 want to ask you something." "Can you not say what you want to say hece 7 " she said. "It is about your going, I suppose "Not exactly; and I cannot talk to you here. Come, Elaine, and hear what I have to say." She walked by his side, slowly enough—as a rule, gay, bright Elaine danced rather than walked, but now her step was slow and languid. He led her to the cushioned chair in the bay window, and placed her in it, standing silently by her side. "Yon have something to say to me," said Elaine at length, "but you seem in no hurry to begin." His heart misgave him; his whole soul shrank from the task. It was cruel to ask her to marry hiM without the bond of love between them. What a pity it was she cared so much for him. As he stood there the the memory of the hour in which he had asked lonie to be his wife recurred te him; his whole heart was in his words then, nom It was only an empty form. He had made his resolve; he would stand by It. If Elaine cared so much for him she should be his wife. He bent his fair, handsome head down gravely' ever the little white hand. It was best to break into the subject at once, while he had the courage to do it. "I brought you here to speak to you about ral going away, Elaine," he said; "and to say to you, I hope that I shall not have to go alone. The VW' tion is sudden, Elaine, but will you go with we as my wife ?" Never, until the day he died, did he forget tbe sudden light that transfigured her face; it abso- lutely dazzled him. "Is it a dream or a reality, Arthur?" she cried. "Are you really asking me to be your wife?" "I am indeed so brave," he answered, with reckless attempt at gaiety. "Is it 'yes' or 'no,' Elaine ? " "I never thought that you loved me, Arthur," she said, catching her breath with a sob. "That is not answering my question, Elaine," be said, evasively. She looked up into his face with the coy, eager delight of a child, murmuring: "I will marry you, if you really wish it, Arthat. It was almost breaking my heart, parting from you." He bent his fair, handsome head and kissed the little, trembling, white hand he held; but be did not kiss her face. "The die is cast ! " he was saying to himself. "I am going to marry Elaine—not for love, but because the girl loves me so dearly it would break • her heart to part from me." (To be continued.)

A HANDSOME GIFT. Mo. Thomas Hodgkins, of Long Island, New York, has given the sum of £20,000 to the Royal Institu- tion, Great Britain, for the promotion of scientific re- search. BOARD OF TRADE RETURNS. The Board cf Trade returns, issued yesterday, show that the imports for Sept. last decreased £2,603,996, compared with the same month last year, whilst the exports for the month also decreased £1,688,684. For the first nine months this year the imports showe4 an 'increase of £696,337 on 1891. whilst the exports for thc Isame period decreased £16,994,608. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT CREWE. -- Yesterday when a luggage train was proceeding, from Crewe to the North Junction an axle of one of the waggons broke, and a portion of the train was thrown off the line. The permanent way was torn up for some distance, and one waggon was smashed. Fortunately the train was going slowly at the time, and no one was injured.
